title: Part 3: Using simulation to understand your data
section: Comparing real, simulated and expected data - continuous distributions
text:
Comparing real, simulated and expected data - continuous distributions
Whatever type of distribution our data is from, this process is very similar.
There are some very minor differences when looking at a continuous variable instead of a discrete variable.
For example, in this paper published in Diversity in 2023, Engelman estimated the body size of an extinct fish, Dunkleosteus terrelli, by looking at fossils and at the correlations between various measurements in other fish.
We will look at the data set they generated by taking various measurements of other fish, in particular, the lamprey Geotria macrostoma and determine if the total length of these fish is normally distributed.
The data, which are identical to Supplementary File S1 from the paper, are saved as data/fish.csv.






Figure 17.1: Dunkleosteus terrelli









Figure 17.2: Geotria macrostoma









ExerciseExercise 5






In your distributions.qmd Quarto file: * Read the file fish.csv into a data frame variable. Use the clean_names() function to clean the column names. * Filter the data to keep only rows where the genus column is equal to Geotria, store the result as a variable named geo. * Plot the column total_length_cm as a histogram
Do you think this data is normally distributed?






AnswerAnswer







# Read the data
fish <- read_csv("data/fish.csv") |> clean_names()

# Filter to keep only the genus Geotria
geo <- fish |> filter(genus == "Geotria")

# Plot a histogram
ggplot(geo, aes(x = total_length_cm)) +
  geom_histogram()








The data looks basically normally distributed.








With continuous data, the probability distribution is described by a probability density function (PDF) rather than a PMF. The theoretical distribution is therefore represented by a continuous curve rather than probabilities at a series of discrete values.
So that our data is comparable with the PDF, we can easily transform our data to show density, rather than counts, using the function after_stat() with the argument density, which we use as a mapping to the geom_histogram() function. after_stat(density) rescales the histogram so that its total area is 1, allowing it to be compared directly with a probability density function.

ggplot(geo, aes(
  x = total_length_cm
)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 30
  )








It might be helpful to compare our data to a perfect, theoretical normal distribution. For a continuous distribution, it’s very easy to add a theoretical distribution to our plot.
The function stat_function() is used to add a continuous curve, based on a function, onto a plot.
The arguments are:

fun - the name of a function
args - a list of the arguments to that function

In our case, the function is dnorm() - the PDF for the normal distribution. The arguments are the two parameters of the normal distribution dnorm() - mean and standard deviation.
So, we would call this function as:
stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean_obs, sd = sd_obs))
Where mean_obs is the mean observed total fish length from our data and sd_obs is the standard deviation of the same data.
We can add this directly to the plot using the same plotting code as before, but with this function as an extra layer.

# Calculate the observed mean and standard deviation
mean_obs <- mean(pull(geo, total_length_cm))
sd_obs <- sd(pull(geo, total_length_cm))

# Draw the plot
ggplot(geo, aes(
  x = total_length_cm
)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 50
  ) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(mean = mean_obs, sd = sd_obs)
  )








One property that can help us describe how the shape of a distribution differs from a normal distribution is skewness - a measure of the asymmetry of the distribution






Figure 17.3: Skewness



We can calculate this using the R functions skewness() from the package moments.
The theoretical normal distribution has a skewness of 0. However, a finite sample drawn from a normal distribution will not usually have a skewness of exactly 0.
The only argument to this function is our observed data vector.

# Pull the total_length_cm column from the geo data frame
body_length <- geo |> pull(total_length_cm)

# Calculate the skewness
skew <- skewness(body_length)
print (skew)

[1] -0.148105


Our observed value is -0.15 — reasonably close to 0. But how close should we expect it to be for a sample of this size? Let’s simulate normally distributed data for comparison.






ExerciseExercise 6






In your distributions.qmd Quarto file:

For 10,000 repeats, using the rnorm() function, generate the same number of data points (you can count how many rows are in the data frame with the function nrow()) as in the geo table with the same mean (function mean()) and standard deviation (function sd()) as Geotria.
Store the skewness for each simulation as a vector.
Calculate the proportion of simulated datasets which were more skewed than the observed data.







AnswerAnswer






For 10,000 repeats, using the rnorm() function, generate the same number of data points as in the geo table with the same mean and standard deviation as Geotria.
Store the skewness for each simulation as a vector.

nrow_obs <- nrow(geo)
mean_obs <- mean(pull(geo, total_length_cm))
sd_obs <- sd(pull(geo, total_length_cm))

skews <- c()

for (i in seq_len(10000)){
  points <- rnorm(nrow_obs, mean = mean_obs, sd = sd_obs)
  skew <- skewness(points)
  skews <- c(skews, skew)
}

skew_df <- tibble(Skewness = skews)

Calculate the proportion of simulated datasets which were more skewed than the observed data.

# Retrieve the observed skewness
body_length <- geo |> pull(total_length_cm)
skew_obs <- skewness(body_length)
# Calculate the absolute value of the observed skewness
abs_skew_obs <- abs(skew_obs)

# Calculate the absolute value of the simulated skewness
abs_skew_sim <- abs(skews)

# Count how many times this is more than our observed skewness
more_than_obs <-sum(abs_skew_sim > abs_skew_obs)

# Count the proportion of times this is more than our observed skewness
skew_prop_more_than_obs <- more_than_obs / 10000

print (skew_prop_more_than_obs)

[1] 0.2592


25.92% of our simulated normal distributions are more skewed than our observed data.
The observed skewness is therefore consistent with what we might expect from a sample of this size drawn from a normal distribution - i.e. if the body length of the whole population of Geotria is normally distributed.

Review
↑ top
We have now used simulation both to model stochastic biological processes and to investigate whether observed biological data are consistent with theoretical probability distributions.






NoteProgramming summary




R uses a consistent set of functions for working with probability distributions:

r...() generates random values from a distribution.
d...() calculates probabilities for discrete distributions or probability densities for continuous distributions.
p...() calculates cumulative probabilities.
q...() calculates quantiles.

rpois() generates random values from a Poisson distribution.
rnorm() generates random values from a normal distribution.
geom_bar() can be used to plot the distribution of discrete observations.
geom_histogram() can be used to plot the distribution of continuous observations.
after_stat(density) rescales a histogram to show probability density rather than counts.
stat_function() can be used to add a theoretical probability density function to a plot.

title: Part 4: Simulation exercises
text:
Distribution 1
Using the skills we’ve built so far, we can now simulate data from any probability distribution implemented in R, whether to compare with observed data, test a hypothesis or model a process.
The data in data/neurons.csv is from this paper, published by Koepcke et al. in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience in 2019.
These authors investigated whether a single neuron can rapidly detect changes in a sensory stimulus by analysing the time between successive action potentials (interspike intervals). The analysis was performed using multiple neurons.
The data in data/neurons.csv come from a single neuron and contain a series of waiting times between successive spikes, measured in seconds.

title: Part 4: Simulation exercises
text:
Distribution 2






NoteExtension Exercise: Distribution 2



Pancreatic islets of Langerhans are clusters of endocrine cells in the pancreas. Individual pancreatic islets vary in size - measurements from human pancreatic islet isolations show a distribution of islet diameters.
In this paper, published in Cell Transplantation in 2009, Buchwald et al. analysed the size composition of human pancreatic islet isolations. The authors had data from more than 200 human islet isolations and looked at the distribution of islet diameters. They found lots of relatively small islets and progressively fewer large ones.
They found that the distribution of individual islet diameters could be described by a Weibull probability distribution with shape parameter κ=1.5 and scale parameter λ=105.
The Weibull probability distribution is available in R using the functions rweibull(), dweibull(), pweibull() and qweibull.
The parameters for rweibull are: * n - number of points to simulate * shape - the shape parameter of the distribution * scale - the scale parameter of the distribution
In your distributions.qmd Quarto file: * Plot a density-scaled histogram of the diameters of 10,000 simulated islets. * Overlay a theoretical Weibull distribution. * During manual assessment, only islets with a diameter of at least 50 μm are included in the standard counting procedure. Given that an islet is included in the count, estimate the probability that its diameter is between 100 and 150 μm.






AnswerAnswer






Plot a density-scaled histogram of the diameters of 10,000 simulated islets.
Overlay a theoretical Weibull distribution.

# Simulate the islets
islet_diams <- rweibull(
  n = 10000,
  shape = 1.5,
  scale = 105
)
# Put them in a data frame
islet_diams_df <- tibble(Islet_Diameter = islet_diams)

# Plot the results as a histogram with an overlaid
# Weibull distribution
ggplot(islet_diams_df, aes(x = Islet_Diameter)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 50,
    fill = "hotpink"
  ) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dweibull,
    args = list(
      shape = 1.5,
      scale = 105
    )
  )








During manual assessment, only islets with a diameter of at least 50 μm are included in the standard counting procedure. Given that an islet is included in the count, estimate the probability that its diameter is between 100 and 150 μm.

# Filter the data frame to keep only islets >= 50 um
islets_over_50 <- islet_diams_df |> filter(Islet_Diameter >= 50)

# Count how many of these there are
n_islets_over_50 <- nrow(islets_over_50)

# Filter the data frame to keep only islets 100-150 um
islets_100_150 <- islet_diams_df |> filter(
  Islet_Diameter >= 100,
  Islet_Diameter <= 150
)
# Count how many of these there are
n_islets_100_150 <- nrow(islets_100_150)

# Calculate the proportion of islets >= 50 um which are 100 to 150 um
prop_counted_islets_100_150 <- n_islets_100_150 / n_islets_over_50
print(prop_counted_islets_100_150)

title: Part 5: Conditional Probability and Bayes’ Theorem
text:
UK cervical screening data
In the UK, cervical screening is routinely offered to any individual with a cervix aged 25 to 64. This screening tests for high risk strains of human papillomavirus (HPV). Members of this group of viruses can damage cells in the cervix and cause cervical cancer. Where tests are positive for high risk HPV (hrHPV), the samples are further tested for abnormal cells and, if abnormal cells are found, additional tests for pre-cancerous cells and cervical cancer are performed.
Therefore, testing for hrHPV can be considered to be a marker for abnormal cervical cells, and therefore for pre-cancerous conditions of the cervix and cervical cancer.
The following data are from this publication, published in 2006 in the British Journal of Cancer (note that this is before routine vaccination against HPV was introduced in the UK. In this study 24,510 people in the UK were screened for hrHPV and cytology was performed in all cases to detect abnormal cells. In this practical we will consider 21,843 of these people - excluding people who had borderline or mild abnormal cytology.
Of these 21,843, 12.1% of people tested positive for hrHPV. 2.1% of people had moderately or severely abnormal cytology, the remainder were normal.
The number of people with and without hrHPV and with and without abnormal cytology are provided in CSV format in data/cm_all_ages.csv.
So far, we’ve calculated proportions using the whole sample of 21,843 individuals. However, the prevalence of moderate/severe abnormal cytology varies considerably with age.

  pull(N_individuals)

Calculate the proportion of people with hrHPV who have abnormal cells.

# Count how many people have hrHPV - positives
hpv_count <- tp + fp

# Calculate the proportion of people with hrHPV who
# also have abnormal cells - true positives / positives
prop_abnormal_given_hpv <- tp / hpv_count
print(prop_abnormal_given_hpv)

[1] 0.1577753


15.78% of people with hrHPV have abnormal cells.
Calculate the proportion of people without hrHPV who have abnormal cells.

# Count how many people don't have hrHPV - negatives
hpv_m_count <- tn + fn

# Calculate the proportion of people who don't have hrHPV who
# do have abnormal cells - false_negatives / negatives
prop_abnormal_given_no_hpv <- fn / hpv_m_count
print(prop_abnormal_given_no_hpv)

[1] 0.002395833


0.24% of people without hrHPV have abnormal cells.
Calculate the proportion of people with abnormal cells who have hrHPV - the sensitivity of the hrHPV as a marker.
\[
\text{Sensitivity} =
\frac{\text{True positives}}
{\text{True positives} + \text{False negatives}}
\]

# Count how many people have abnormal cells -
# true positives and false negatives
ab_count <- tp + fn

# Calculate the proportion of people who have
# abnormal cells who also have hpv
prop_hpv_given_abnormal <- tp / ab_count
print(prop_hpv_given_abnormal)

The sensitivity of HPV status as a test for abnormal cells is 90.06%.
Calculate the proportion of people who have normal cells and don’t have hrHPV - the specificity of hrHPV as a marker.
\[
\text{Specificity} =
\frac{\text{True negatives}}
{\text{True negatives} + \text{False positives}}
\]

# Count how many people have normal cells -
# true negatives and false positives
n_count <- tn + fp

# Calculate the proportion of people who have
# normal cells who don't have hpv
prop_no_hpv_given_normal <- tn / n_count
print(prop_no_hpv_given_normal)

The specificity of HPV status as a test for abnormal cells is 89.59%.

ExerciseExercise 2






In your HPV.qmd Quarto file:

For each of these age groups, simulate a sample of 10,000 individuals with the appropriate prevalence of moderate/severe cytology.
For the individuals in your simulation with and without moderate/severe cytology, simulate the presence of HPV based on the frequencies calculated in exercise 1.
In each iteration, store the number of people with HPV, the number of people with abnormal cells and the number of people with abnormal cells and HPV in a data frame.
Use your simulated data to estimate the probability that an individual in each group with hrHPV has moderate-or-worse abnormal cytology.
Use your simulated data to estimate the probability that an individual in each group with moderate-or-worse abnormal cytology has hrHPV.
Why does the probability that an individual in each group with hrHPV has moderate-or-worse abnormal cytology differ so much, even though the sensitivity and specificity of hrHPV as a marker were kept constant?







AnswerAnswer






For each of these age groups, simulate a sample of 10,000 individuals with the appropriate prevalence of moderate/severe cytology.
For the individuals in your simulation with and without moderate/severe cytology, simulate the presence of HPV based on the frequencies calculated in exercise 1.
In each iteration, store the number of people with HPV, the number of people with abnormal cells and the number of people with abnormal cells and HPV in a data frame.

prevs <- c(0.0508, 0.0181, 0.0047)

n_sim <- 10000
results <- tibble()

for (prop_abnormal in prevs) {
  # Simulate a population of people with normal and
  # abnormal cells at the population rate
  # 1 = abnormal
  # 0 = normal
  cyt_statuses <- rbinom(n_sim, 1, prop_abnormal)

  # Count how many people have abnormal cells
  n_abnormal <- sum(cyt_statuses == 1)
  n_normal <- sum(cyt_statuses == 0)

  # For the people with abnormal cells, simulate HPV
  # presence based on the proportion of people with HPV
  # given abnormal cells calculated in ex1.

  hpv_statuses_abnormal <- rbinom(
    n_abnormal, 1,
    prop_hpv_given_abnormal
  )

  # For the people with normal cells, simulate HPV
  # presence

  # Calculate the proportion of people with HPV given
  # normal cells
  prop_hpv_given_normal <- 1 - prop_no_hpv_given_normal

  hpv_statuses_normal <- rbinom(
    n_normal, 1,
    prop_hpv_given_normal
  )

  # How many people have HPV
  n_hpv <- sum(hpv_statuses_normal == 1) + sum(hpv_statuses_abnormal == 1)

  # How many people have HPV and abnormal cells - true positives
  n_hpv_abnormal <- sum(hpv_statuses_abnormal == 1)

  # Generate a row for the data frame with these results
  current <- tibble(
    Prevalence = prop_abnormal,
    N_Abnormal = n_abnormal,
    N_HPV = n_hpv,
    N_TP = n_hpv_abnormal
  )

  # Add this result to the data frame
  results <- results |> bind_rows(current)
}

# Add a column to the data frame with the age ranges
# .before = 1 - put it before the first column

results <- results |> mutate(age_group = c(
  "20-29",
  "30-49",
  "50-64"
), .before = 1)

  Abnormal_given_hrHPV = N_TP / N_HPV,

)

Why does the probability that an individual in each group with hrHPV has moderate-or-worse abnormal cytology differ so much, even though the sensitivity and specificity of hrHPV as a marker were kept constant?
Because the prevalence of abnormal cells changes so much between the groups. The sensitivity of the test tells us the probability the person will test positive if they have the disease and the specificity tells us the probability they will test negative if they don’t have the disease. The ratio of people who do and don’t have the disease differs between the three samples.














NoteExtension exercise: Cervical cancer



We can extend this simulation to consider cervical cancer as an outcome, rather than just abnormal cells.
Based on this paper published in Cytopathology in 2016 and also based on UK individuals, the positive predictive value of moderate or severely abnormal cells for cervical cancer is:

1.5% for people aged 20-29
3.4% for people aged 30-49
5.1% for people aged 50-64

(Note that these are estimates, as this paper uses slightly different age ranges)
This means that, based on this sample, for example, 1.5% of people aged 20-29 with at least moderately abnormal cells will then be diagnosed with cervical cancer. In this study no-one of any age with normal cells was diagnosed with cervical cancer.
Extend your simulation to calculate the probability that a 24 year old who is HPV positive and has a cervix would be diagnosed with cervical cancer on further testing (assuming prevalence is constant across the 20-29 age group).

results_cc <- tibble()
prop_cc_given_abnormal <- 0.015
prop_abnormal <- 0.0508

# Simulate a population of people with normal and
# abnormal cells at the population rate for age 20-29
# 1 = abnormal
# 0 = normal
cyt_statuses <- rbinom(n_sim, 1, prop_abnormal)

# Count how many people have abnormal cells
n_abnormal <- sum(cyt_statuses == 1)
n_normal <- sum(cyt_statuses == 0)
  
# For the people with abnormal cells, simulate HPV
# presence based on the proportion of people with HPV
# given abnormal cells calculated in ex1.
hpv_statuses_abnormal <- rbinom(
  n_abnormal, 1,
  prop_hpv_given_abnormal
)

# For the people with normal cells, simulate HPV
# presence based on the proportion of people with HPV
# given abnormal cells calculated in ex1.
hpv_statuses_normal <- rbinom(
  n_normal, 1,
  prop_hpv_given_normal
)

# Only the abnormal cells people can have HPV in this example
# For the people with abnormal cells, simulate cervical
# cancer with a prevalence of 0.015
cc_statuses_abnormal <- rbinom(
  n_abnormal, 1,
  prop_cc_given_abnormal
)
# How many people have HPV
n_hpv <- sum(hpv_statuses_abnormal == 1) + sum(hpv_statuses_normal == 1)

# How many people have HPV and cervical cancer
n_hpv_cc <- sum(cc_statuses_abnormal == 1 & hpv_statuses_abnormal == 1)

# What proportion of people with HPV have cervical cancer
prop_cc <- n_hpv_cc / n_hpv

print(prop_cc)

Under this simplified model, we estimate that 0.14% of HPV-positive individuals aged 20–29 would be diagnosed with cervical cancer.

This is a simplified model designed to explore conditional probability and should not be interpreted as a model of an individual’s clinical risk.

title: Part 5 - Bonus: Sampling from a user-defined probability distribution
text:
Sampling from a user defined probability distribution
This whole page is bonus content
Earlier, we used functions such as rbinom(), rpois() and rnorm() to simulate data from named probability distributions. However, sometimes we may want to simulate from a probability distribution for which R does not provide a built-in random-sampling function, or from a PDF that we have defined ourselves.
In R, it is possible to simulate data from a user-defined probability distribution using the package Runuran.
library(Runuran)
For example, cats like to sit on keyboards, particularly if they are currently being used. Let’s say a researcher has developed a probability density function describing the position at which a cat’s centre of mass occurs along a 40-cm keyboard, measured as distance in cm from the left edge.
\[
f(x) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{3x(40-x)}{32000}, & 0 \leq x \leq 40 \\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
Let’s plot just the function.
Here, instead of giving the argument fun our function name, we directly give it our cat PDF.
ggplot() +
  stat_function(
    fun = function(x) {
      3 * x * (40 - x) / 32000
    },
    xlim = c(0, 40)
  ) +
  xlab("Distance from Left Edge") +
  ylab("Density")
As expected, cats like to sit in the middle where they can obscure the most keys and, ideally, block the view of the screen.
For a function to be a valid PDF, its total area must equal 1. We can check this in R using integrate(). integrate() takes 3 arguments - the PDF, lower - the lower bound - and upper - the upper bound.
cat_int <- integrate(function(x) {
  3 * x * (40 - x) / 32000
}, lower = 0, upper = 40)
print(cat_int)

1 with absolute error < 1.1e-14
The total area under this curve is 1 - so the function is valid.
Using our probability density function, let’s simulate the positions of 10,000 cats, then estimate the probability that the centre of the cat is within the central 10 cm of the keyboard.
First, we use the function pinv.new() to create a random number generator which can sample values from a continuous distribution described by a user-defined PDF.
The arguments are: * pdf - the PDF * lb - the lower bound, in our case 0 * ub - the upper bound, in our case 40
cat_gen <- pinv.new(
  pdf = function(x) {
    3 * x * (40 - x) / 32000
  },
  lb = 0,
  ub = 40
)
Now, to simulate data from this distribution, we use the function ur().
cat_positions <- ur(cat_gen,
  n = 10000
)
Let’s plot our cats. First, we need to put the data in a data frame.
cat_df <- tibble(Position = cat_positions)
ggplot(cat_df, aes(x = Position)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 50) +
  stat_function(
    fun = function(x) {
      3 * x * (40 - x) / 32000
    }
  )
Finally, let’s estimate the probability that a cat will sit within the central 10 cm of the keyboard. The middle 10 cm lies between 15 cm and 25 cm from the left edge.
middle_only <- cat_df |> filter(
  Position >= 15,
  Position <= 25
)
prop_middle <- nrow(middle_only) / nrow(cat_df)
print(prop_middle)

[1] 0.3628
Based on our simulation, cats will sit in the middle 10 cm of the keyboard approximately 36.28% of the time.

text:
Figure 20.1: Example data point



























ExerciseExercise 1






Some cat parents like to, for their own amusement, pile objects onto their sleeping cat, a game known as cat buckaroo.






Figure 20.2: Example data point



Cats will tolerate this to a certain extent but, at some point, will get up and shake the objects off. The weight of objects the cat will tolerate varies considerably between cats.
Cats appear to fall into two broad groups: those that almost immediately object to this game, and those that will tolerate a substantial pile before taking action. A researcher proposes the following probability density function for the total weight of objects a sleeping cat will tolerate before shaking them off.
\[
f(x) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{1-\cos\left(\frac{4\pi x}{1000}\right)}{1000},
& 0 \leq x \leq 1000 \\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]






Note



To use pi in R, you can just type pi.

print(pi)

[1] 3.141593


To calculate a cosine you can use the function cos() with one argument, the number for which you want to calculate the cosine.


In your distributions.qmd Quarto file:

Plot this function.
Check it is a valid PDF.
Create a random number generator which can sample values from the distribution described by this PDF.
Simulate 10,000 values.
A cat has already tolerated 500 g of objects. Estimate the probability that it will tolerate the addition of a 75 g Yoda figurine without shaking everything off.







Figure 20.3: Example data point









AnswerAnswer






Plot this function.

ggplot() +
  stat_function(
    fun = function(x) {
      (1 - cos(4 * pi * x / 1000)) / 1000
    },
    xlim = c(0, 1000)
  ) +
  xlab("Weight of objects") +
  ylab("Density")








Check it is a valid PDF.

cataroo_int <- integrate(
  function(x) {
    (1 - cos(4 * pi * x / 1000)) / 1000
  },
  lower = 0,
  upper = 1000
)
print(cataroo_int)

1 with absolute error < 7.3e-10


The area under the curve is 1 so this is a valid PDF.
Create a random number generator which can sample values from the distribution described by this PDF.

cataroo_gen <- pinv.new(
  pdf = function(x) {
    (1 - cos(4 * pi * x / 1000)) / 1000
  },
  lb = 0,
  ub = 1000
)

[UNU.RAN - warning] NaN occured: tail probability gives NaN --> assume 0.
[UNU.RAN - warning] NaN occured: tail probability gives NaN --> assume 0.


Simulate 10,000 values.

cat_tolerance <- ur(cataroo_gen,
  n = 10000
)

A cat has already tolerated 500 g of objects. Estimate the probability that it will tolerate the addition of a 75 g Yoda figurine without shaking everything off.

cat_tolerance_df <- tibble(Tolerance = cat_tolerance)

# Find all the cats who tolerated at least 500g
over_500 <- cat_tolerance_df |> filter(Tolerance >= 500)

# Find all the cats who tolerated at least 575g
over_575 <- cat_tolerance_df |> filter(Tolerance >= 575)

# Calculate the proportion of cats who tolerated at least 500g who will tolerate at least 575g.
prop <- nrow(over_575) / nrow(over_500)

print(prop)

[1] 0.9782

If a cat has tolerated the addition of 500g of objects, there is an estimated 97.82% probability they will tolerate an additional 75g Yoda figurine.

title: Part 1: Estimators
text:
The dataset
The dataset we will use in this practical is pan-trap survey data from the UK Pollinator Monitoring Scheme. In this scheme, multiple pan-traps are set in each of a set of specific 1km squares across the UK. On four days each summer, volunteers will set out traps for six hours, then send the insects to be counted. Flowering plants within a 2m radius of the trap are also recorded.
The data from the scheme is provided as data per trap, for this practical we have amalgamated the data across all dates and across each 1km square. The preprocessing of the data is described in XXXX.
You have been provided with four data files:

title: Part 1: Estimators
text:
In the insect counts CSV file - data/insect_counts.csv each row represents a combination of an insect species and a sampling site, and the total number of times that insect was observed at that site. Many of the counts will be zero.
In the flower counts CSV file - data/flower_counts.csv each row reprsents a combination of a flower species and a sampling site, plus TRUE or FALSE depending if that flower was ever observed within 2m of the site.
In the site metadata CSV file - data/site_metadata.csv, each row represents a single 1km square sampling site. The data frame contains information about the geographical location, plus land use and climate at the sample site. Additional climate data has been added based WorldClim data, which has detailed climate data by square averaged from 1970-2000. Various additional statistics have been calculated based on the information in the original data frame.
In the insect metadata CSV file - data/insect_metadata.csv, each row represents a single species of bee or hoverfly and its common name (where available), order and family. Additional data about the mass and length of the insects has been added from the pollimetry R package.
In the flower metadata CSV file - data/flower_metadata.csv, each row represents a single species of plant and its common name (where available), order and family.

title: Part 1: Estimators
text:
Estimators
Let’s concentrate on a single aspect of the data for now - the species richness, measured as the number of unique species.
Across the whole dataset, we know the total number of unique species - we have one species for each row in our insect metadata data frame.

n_unique_species <- nrow(insect_metadata)
print(n_unique_species)

[1] 255


There are 255 unique species.
The data we have here is only a sample of the whole population, but for this exercise, we will treat the complete dataset as a pseudo-population and explore what happens when we take samples from this population.
Let’s say we wanted to estimate the total species richness across the full data set based on 20 sites and we have three possible estimators:

Observed richness - total number of unique species across 20 sites
Scaled observed richness - total number of unique species across 20 sites * (total number of sites / 20)
The Chao1 richness estimator, which uses the number of rare species in the sample to estimate how many species may have gone undetected.

First let’s take a sample of 20 random sites.

random_sites <- site_metadata |>
  distinct(x1km_square) |>
  slice_sample(n = 20) |>
  pull(x1km_square)

Now we can extract these rows from our insect counts data frame. For this part of the practical, we’re not interested in insects with a count of 0.

insect_sample <- insect_counts |>
  filter(
    x1km_square %in% random_sites,
    n_observed != 0
  )

gt(head(insect_sample))

Observed richness
The observed richness is just the total number of unique species observed across all sites.

obs_rich <- insect_sample |>
  distinct(species) |>
  pull(species)
n_obs_rich <- length(obs_rich)
print(n_obs_rich)

[1] 183


The observed richness estimator for this sample is 183.


Scaled observed richness
The scaled observed richness is the total number of unique species observed across all sites, multiplied by (total number of sites / number of sites in sample).

n_sites_sample <- 20
scaled_obs_rich <- n_obs_rich * (site_count / n_sites_sample)
print(scaled_obs_rich)

[1] 695.4


The scaled observed richness estimator for this sample is 695.


Chao1 estimator
The Chao1 estimator estimates unseen species based on the number of species represented only once or twice in your sample.
\[
\hat{S}_{Chao1} = S_{obs} + \frac{f_1^2}{2f_2}
\]
where:

\(S_{obs}\) is the number of species observed in the sample.
\(f_1\) is the number of species observed exactly once (singletons).
\(f_2\) is the number of species observed exactly twice (doubletons).







Note



You do not need to remember this - it is just an example of an estimator.



obs_per_insect <- insect_sample |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(n_total = sum(n_observed))

once <- obs_per_insect |> filter(n_total == 1)
twice <- obs_per_insect |> filter(n_total == 2)

n_once <- nrow(once)
n_twice <- nrow(twice)

chao <- n_obs_rich + ((n_once^2) / (2 * n_twice))
print(chao)

[1] 215.3269


The chao1 estimator for this sample is 215.
None of these did a particularly good job of finding our real value of 255.
However, you can’t measure how good an estimator is based on a single sample. Let’s try simulation and generate multiple samples.
Remember (from the lectures): An unbiased estimator gives the correct value on average across repeated samples. The efficiency of an estimator is determined by its variance: estimators with lower variance give more consistent estimates. Mean square error (MSE) combines bias and variance and measures how far, overall, estimates tend to be from the true value.






ExerciseExercise 2






Using a for loop, with 10,000 iterations (this might take a minute or two to run).

Take a sample of 20 sites, then extract the insect counts for these sites from the data frame.
Calculate observed richness, scaled observed richness and chao1 for each sample.
Store the results for each estimator in a separate vector.
Combine these into a data frame.
For each estimator:

Calculate the bias, as the difference between the mean value across samples and the real value from our pseudo population.
Calculate the variance.
Calculate the mean square error.

Which estimator would you use, if any?







AnswerAnswer






Take a sample of 20 sites, then extract the insect counts for these sites from the data frame.
Calculate observed richness, scaled observed richness and chao1 for each sample.
Store the results for each estimator in a separate vector.

obs_rich_vec <- c()
scaled_obs_rich_vec <- c()
chao_vec <- c()

# Loop for 10,000 iterations
for (i in seq_len(10000)) {
  # Sample 20 sites
  random_sites <- site_metadata |>
    distinct(x1km_square) |>
    slice_sample(n = 20) |>
    pull(x1km_square)

  # Extract the insect counts for these sites
  insect_sample <- insect_counts |>
    filter(
      x1km_square %in% random_sites,
      n_observed != 0
    )

  # Calculate observed richness
  obs_rich <- insect_sample |>
    distinct(species) |>
    pull(species)
  n_obs_rich <- length(obs_rich)
  # Store
  obs_rich_vec <- c(obs_rich_vec, n_obs_rich)

  # Calculate the scaled observed richness
  scaled_obs_rich <- n_obs_rich * (site_count / 20)
  # Store
  scaled_obs_rich_vec <- c(scaled_obs_rich_vec, scaled_obs_rich)

  # Calculate Chao1
  obs_per_insect <- insect_sample |>
    group_by(species) |>
    summarise(n_total = sum(n_observed))

  once <- obs_per_insect |> filter(n_total == 1)
  twice <- obs_per_insect |> filter(n_total == 2)

  n_once <- nrow(once)
  n_twice <- nrow(twice)

  chao <- n_obs_rich + ((n_once^2) / (2 * n_twice))
  # Store
  chao_vec <- c(chao_vec, chao)
}

Combine these into a data frame.

estimator_df <- tibble(
  Observed = obs_rich_vec,
  Scaled_Observed = scaled_obs_rich_vec,
  Chao1 = chao_vec)

For each estimator:
Calculate the bias
Calculate the efficiency
Calculate the mean square error.

estimator_summary <- estimator_df |>
  summarise(
    Bias_Observed = mean(Observed) - n_unique_species,
    Bias_Scaled_Observed = mean(Scaled_Observed) - n_unique_species,
    Bias_Chao1 = mean(Chao1) - n_unique_species,
    Eff_Observed = var(Observed),
    Eff_Scaled_Observed = var(Scaled_Observed),
    Eff_Chao1 = var(Chao1),
    MSE_Observed = mean((Observed - n_unique_species)^2),
    MSE_Scaled_Observed =mean((Scaled_Observed - n_unique_species)^2),
    MSE_Chao1 = mean((Chao1 - n_unique_species)^2)
  )
gt(estimator_summary)

Which estimator would you use, if any?
Of the three, the Chao1 estimator has the lowest mean square error, however it is still has a negative bias and a low efficiency.








Plotting our simulated estimators also provides a lot of information.
We can combine all three estimators into a single plot, first we need to convert the data from wide to long format (see Long and wide formats).
The function everything() tells R to pivot all of the columns in the table. A new column, estimator will be created to specify if each row is an observed, scaled observed or chao1 estimator.

estimator_long <- estimator_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "estimator",
    values_to = "estimate"
  )

gt(head(estimator_long))

Now, let’s plot the values of each estimator as histograms.
The function facet_wrap() splits the data from a single data frame into multiple plots, based on the values in a categorical column. The first argument should be the variable you would like to facet by, preceded by a ~ symbol. The argument scales = "free" means that each plot can have a different scale bar - by default they are all the same.
The function geom_vline() adds a vertical line at a specific point, specified by the argument xintercept. In this case, the line is at our pseudo-population total species richness.

ggplot(estimator_long, aes(x = estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=50) +
  facet_wrap(~ estimator, scales = "free") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = n_unique_species, color='red')








Here it is clear again that none of these are great estimators, but that Chao1 is probably the best.






Note



Sometimes an estimator is bad because the sample size is too small, sometimes it’s just bad. Let’s try taking 50 sites per sample, instead of 20.
The code below is identical to the above except for samples of 50 sites.

obs_rich_vec_50 <- c()
scaled_obs_rich_vec_50 <- c()
chao_vec_50 <- c()

# Loop for 10,000 iterations
for (i in seq_len(10000)) {
  # Sample 50 sites
  random_sites <- site_metadata |>
    distinct(x1km_square) |>
    slice_sample(n = 50) |>
    pull(x1km_square)

  # Extract the insect counts for these sites
  insect_sample <- insect_counts |>
    filter(
      x1km_square %in% random_sites,
      n_observed != 0
    )

  # Calculate observed richness
  obs_rich <- insect_sample |>
    distinct(species) |>
    pull(species)
  n_obs_rich <- length(obs_rich)
  # Store
  obs_rich_vec_50 <- c(obs_rich_vec_50, n_obs_rich)

  # Calculate the scaled observed richness
  scaled_obs_rich <- n_obs_rich * (site_count / 50)
  # Store
  scaled_obs_rich_vec_50 <- c(scaled_obs_rich_vec_50, scaled_obs_rich)

  # Calculate Chao1
  obs_per_insect <- insect_sample |>
    group_by(species) |>
    summarise(n_total = sum(n_observed))

  once <- obs_per_insect |> filter(n_total == 1)
  twice <- obs_per_insect |> filter(n_total == 2)

  n_once <- nrow(once)
  n_twice <- nrow(twice)

  chao <- n_obs_rich + ((n_once^2) / (2 * n_twice))
  # Store
  chao_vec_50 <- c(chao_vec_50, chao)
}

estimator_df_50 <- tibble(
  Observed = obs_rich_vec_50,
  Scaled_Observed = scaled_obs_rich_vec_50,
  Chao1 = chao_vec_50)

Now we can look at the results.

  summarise(
    Bias_Observed = mean(Observed) - n_unique_species,
    Bias_Scaled_Observed = mean(Scaled_Observed) - n_unique_species,

    Eff_Scaled_Observed = var(Scaled_Observed),

    MSE_Scaled_Observed =mean((Scaled_Observed - n_unique_species)^2),

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Choosing a test
Now we have a hypothesis to investigate:

Alternative hypothesis: Minimum temperature is different at sites where H. tumulorum is present than at sites where it is absent.
Null hypothesis: Mean minimum temperature is the same at sites where H. tumulorum is present and absent.







Important



We developed our hypothesis that H. tumulorum prefers sites with a higher minimum temperature after looking at these data, and we’re about to use the same data to test that hypothesis. This is sometimes called HARKing — Hypothesizing After the Results are Known.
Ideally, we would now test our hypothesis using a new dataset. However, given the limitations of this practical, we will instead look for evidence of an association in this dataset.


We have a continuous response variable and a categorical explanatory variable - maybe we can use a t-test.
There are various assumptions which underlie a t-test - we’ll come back to these later in the practical. For the moment, assume these assumptions are met.

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Running statistical tests in R
In R statistical functions, ~ is used to specify a formula describing the relationship between variables.
The basic structure is response ~ explanatory, which you can read as “response as a function of explanatory variable”.
In our example above, the response variable is minimum temperature and the explanatory variable is presence or absence of H. tumulorum bees.






Note



“Explanatory” here means the variable we’re using to explain/describe variation in the response statistically, not necessarily a biological cause - we’re not claiming that the bees are affecting the temperature.


To run a t-test in R, the function is t.test().
The first argument is our formula - response ~ explanatory, or in this case, min_temp_coldest_month ~ detected. We need two additional arguments:

data = ht_temp_df - this is the data frame containing the data.
var.equal = TRUE - run a standard t-test, the default in R is to assume unequal variance and run a Welch’s t-test.


ttest_ht_temp <- t.test(min_temp_coldest_month ~ detected,
  data = ht_temp_df,
  var.equal = TRUE
)
print(ttest_ht_temp)


    Two Sample t-test

data:  min_temp_coldest_month by detected
t = -5.7259, df = 74, p-value = 2.073e-07
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group FALSE and group TRUE is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -1.7010818 -0.8228055
sample estimates:
mean in group FALSE  mean in group TRUE 
          0.1128519           1.3747955 


The p-value for a t-test is the probability of a test statistic at least as far from zero as the value calculated from our data, if we drew values from a t-distribution with the specified number of degrees of freedom.
For a standard two-sample t-test, the degrees of freedom are the total number of observations minus the number of group means estimated. Here we have 76 observations and estimate two means, so the degrees of freedom are 76 - 2 = 74.
So, to fully describe our t-test output we need to include at least the following:

Test statistic: t
Degrees of freedom: df
p-value: p-value

In addition to the test statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value, we should describe the size and direction of the observed difference. R reports the two group means, from which we can calculate the difference between the means.
We could therefore report our results here as:

There is evidence that mean minimum temperature is higher at sites where H. tumulorum is present than at sites where it is absent (\(t\)(74) = -5.73, \(p\) = 2.07e-07, mean difference [absent − present] = -1.26°C). This means we can reject our null hypothesis.

This doesn’t mean that our alternative hypothesis is definitely true for the population, but based on this sample the evidence supports it.

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Extension exercise - the t-distribution






Note



I stated above that: “The p-value for a t-test is the probability of a test statistic at least as far from zero as the value calculated from our data, if we drew values from a t-distribution with the specified number of degrees of freedom”.
The t-distribution is just a probability distribution, so we can simulate and visualise it in R using the same methods we learned for other probability distributions (Part 4: Simulation exercises).
In your pollinators.qmd Quarto file:

Simulate a sample of 1000 observations from t-distribution with 74 degrees of freedom. You can draw a random sample from a t-distribution with the function rt with the arguments n - number of observations and df degrees of freedom.
Create a dataframe where this set of observations forms a column.
Plot the results using the ggplot layer geom_density().
Calculate an approximated p-value using your simulated data - the proportion of observations which are at least 5.726 from zero in either direction. You can extract the test statistic from the t-test as ttest_ht_temp$statistic.
Calculate the exact p-value using the t-distribution cumulative probability function pt().







AnswerAnswer






Simulate a sample of 1000 observations from t-distribution with 74 degrees of freedom. You can draw a random sample from a t-distribution with the function rt with the arguments n - number of observations and df degrees of freedom.

df74 <- rt(1000, df = 74)

Create a dataframe where this set of observations forms a column.

t_dist <- tibble(simulated = df74)

Plot the results using the ggplot layer geom_density().

ggplot(
  t_dist,
  aes(x = simulated)
) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(ttest_ht_temp$statistic, -ttest_ht_temp$statistic), color = "red")








Calculate an approximated p-value using your simulated data - the proportion of observations which are at least 5.726 from zero in either direction. You can extract the test statistic from the t-test as ttest_ht_temp$statistic.

p_lower_sim <- sum(t_dist$simulated <= ttest_ht_temp$statistic)
p_upper_sim <- sum(t_dist$simulated >= -ttest_ht_temp$statistic)

p_sim <- (p_lower_sim + p_upper_sim) / nrow(t_dist)

print(p_sim)

[1] 0


With 1000 simulations your value will almost certainly be zero.






NoteBonus question: Probability



What is the probability of getting a value which is not zero here given the p-value calculated by R above of 2.07e-07.






AnswerAnswer







prob_no_extreme <- (1 - ttest_ht_temp$p.value)^1000
prob_at_least_one <- 1 - prob_no_extreme

print(prob_at_least_one)

[1] 0.0002073172


There is a 0.0207% probability of observing at least one simulated value this extreme when drawing 1,000 points from a t-distribution with 74 degrees of freedom.






Calculate the exact p-value using the t-distribution cumulative probability function pt().

p_lower <- pt(ttest_ht_temp$statistic, 74)
p_upper <- 1 - pt(-ttest_ht_temp$statistic, 74)

pval <- p_lower + p_upper

print(pval)

           t 
2.073387e-07 


This should be the exact p-value calculated in our t-test.

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Confidence intervals
In our description of the t-test output above, something is missing - it is also worth looking at our confidence interval here. This data is provided in our t-test summary above.
Lower: -1.7011
Upper: -0.8228
A 95% confidence interval means that if we repeatedly sampled from the population and calculated a 95% confidence interval in the same way each time, 95% of those intervals would contain the true population value. In this case, the true population value is the true difference between the mean minimum annual temperature at sites where H. tumulorum is present and at sites where it is absent.
For a two-sided test at the 5% significance level, if the 95% confidence interval for the difference between the means does not contain zero, we can reject the null hypothesis that the mean difference is zero. Here, our confidence interval does not contain zero, which agrees with our conclusion based on the p-value.
We should add this to our conclusion above:

There is evidence that mean minimum temperature is higher at sites where H. tumulorum is present than at sites where it is absent (\(t\)(74) = -5.73, \(p\) = 2.07e-07, mean difference [absent − present] = -1.26°C, 95% CI [-1.7, -0.82]°C). This means we can reject our null hypothesis.







ExerciseExercise 2






“A 95% confidence interval means that if we repeatedly sampled from the population and calculated a 95% confidence interval in the same way each time, 95% of those intervals would contain the true population value. In this case, the true population value is the true difference between the mean minimum annual temperature at sites where H. tumulorum is present and at sites where it is absent.”
Let’s check using simulation. If we simulate samples from populations with known means, we know the “true” difference between means of the source populations.
To simplify this process, let’s first calculate the mean, standard deviation and sample size for sites with and without H. tumulorum. This is straightforward using the group_by() and summarise() functions.

ht_temp_summ <- ht_temp_df |>
  group_by(detected) |>
  summarise(
    mean = mean(min_temp_coldest_month),
    sd = sd(min_temp_coldest_month),
    count = n()
  )

# Separate present and absent sites
present <- ht_temp_summ |>
  filter(detected == TRUE)

absent <- ht_temp_summ |>
  filter(detected == FALSE)

gt(ht_temp_summ)







detected
mean
sd
count




FALSE
0.1128519
1.0805316
37


TRUE
1.3747955
0.8305563
39







Next, in your pollinators.qmd Quarto file:

1,000 times:

Simulate two samples drawn from a normal distribution:

one with the same mean, standard deviation and sample size as the sites with H. tumulorum
one with the same mean, standard deviation and sample size as the sites without H. tumulorum.

Put the data for the two samples into a data frame in long format as follows:


# Let's assume your vectors are in variables named s1 and s2
# rep is used to add the sample names to the data frame

df <- tibble(
sample = c(
  rep("sample_1", length(s1)),
  rep("sample_2", length(s2))
),
min_temp_coldest_month = c(s1, s2)
)


For each pair of simulated samples, use a t-test to calculate the difference between the sample means, and its 95% confidence interval.
Extract the confidence interval


# If the result of your t-test is stored as ttest_res
ci_lower <- ttest_res$conf.int[1]
ci_upper <- ttest_res$conf.int[2]


Record whether the confidence interval contains the true difference between the two population means. Because we specified the means of our simulated populations ourselves, we know what this value is: 1.2619







Note



The function between(value, lower, upper) will tell you if value is between lower and upper.



Store TRUE or FALSE in a vector depending on the result.

Calculate the percentage of the 1,000 confidence intervals that contain the true difference.







AnswerAnswer






1,000 times:

Simulate two samples drawn from a normal distribution:

one with the same mean, standard deviation and sample size as the sites with H. tumulorum
one with the same mean, standard deviation and sample size as the sites without H. tumulorum.

Put the data for the two samples into a data frame in long format.
For each pair of simulated samples, use a t-test to calculate the difference between the sample means and its 95% confidence interval.
Extract the confidence interval.
Determine whether the confidence interval contains the true difference between the two population means.
Store TRUE or FALSE in a vector depending on the result.


# Find the real difference for comparison
true_diff <- pull(present, mean) - pull(absent, mean)

# Vector to store the results
res_vec <- c()

for (i in seq_len(1000)) {
  # Simulate the two samples
  sample_present <- rnorm(pull(present, count), mean = pull(present, mean), sd = pull(present, sd))
  sample_absent <- rnorm(pull(absent, count), mean = pull(absent, mean), sd = pull(absent, sd))

  # Put the results into a data frame
  df <- tibble(
    sample = c(
      rep("sample_1", length(sample_present)),
      rep("sample_2", length(sample_absent))
    ),
    min_temp_coldest_month = c(sample_present, sample_absent)
  )

  # Run the t-test
  ttest_res <- t.test(min_temp_coldest_month ~ sample,
    data = df,
    var.equal = TRUE
  )

  # Extract the confidence interval
  ci_lower <- ttest_res$conf.int[1]
  ci_upper <- ttest_res$conf.int[2]

  # Check if the result is in the confidence interval or not
  res_in_ci <- between(true_diff, ci_lower, ci_upper)

  # Store the result
  res_vec <- c(res_vec, res_in_ci)
}

Calculate the percentage of the 1,000 confidence intervals that contain the true difference.

perc <- (sum(res_vec) / length(res_vec)) * 100
print(perc)

[1] 94.6


In this simulation, the confidence interval included the true difference 94.6% of the time - very similar to our expectation.














NoteExtension - the t-distribution and confidence intervals



We can revisit our simulated t-distribution above to understand how confidence intervals are calculated.
For a 95% confidence interval, we want the central 95% of the t-distribution. This leaves 2.5% of the distribution in each tail.
In our t_dist data frame there are 1,000 observations sampled from a t-distribution with 74 degrees of freedom.

ggplot(
  t_dist,
  aes(x = simulated)
) +
  geom_density()








To calculate our confidence interval, we want the middle 95% of values from this distribution.
With our simulated data, we can extract these using summarize() and then the quantile() function with the data column as the first argument and the quantile we want to extract as the second. The \(x\) quantile is the value below which \(x\) proportion of the observations fall.

quantile_df <- t_dist |>
  summarise(
    lower = quantile(simulated, 0.025),
    upper = quantile(simulated, 0.975)
  )
gt(quantile_df)







lower
upper




-1.98262
1.878672







Let’s add these to our density plot.

ggplot(
  t_dist,
  aes(x = simulated)
) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(pull(quantile_df, lower), pull(quantile_df, upper)), color = "blue")








We can also calculate the exact values using the function qt().

lower_exact <- qt(0.025, 74)
upper_exact <- qt(0.975, 74)

print(lower_exact)

[1] -1.992543

print(upper_exact)

[1] 1.992543


The absolute values of these exact values should be identical to each other.

ggplot(
  t_dist,
  aes(x = simulated)
) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(lower_exact, upper_exact), color = "orange")








Because the t-distribution is symmetric, the two exact quantiles have the same absolute value. This value is called the critical t-value, often written \(t*\). These values are measured on the t-distribution. To calculate a confidence interval for our estimated difference between means, we need to convert \(t*\) into the units of our response variable.
We do this by multiplying \(t*\) by the standard error of our t-test. We can access from our t-test above using ttest_ht_temp$stderr.

tstar <- upper_exact
SE <- ttest_ht_temp$stderr

confint_rv_units <- tstar * SE

print(confint_rv_units)

[1] 0.4391381


This tells us how far we need to go above and below our estimated difference between means to obtain the 95% confidence interval.

diff_means <- pull(absent, mean) - pull(present, mean)

lower_cint <- diff_means - confint_rv_units
upper_cint <- diff_means + confint_rv_units

print(c(lower_cint, upper_cint))

[1] -1.7010818 -0.8228055


This gives us our lower value of -1.7011 and upper value of -0.8228 as above.

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Linear models
The comparison we have just made can also be represented using a linear model.
As you know, a simple linear model can be written as:
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \epsilon
\] where:

\(y\) is the response variable - minimum temperature
\(x\) is the explanatory variable - H. tumulorum present or absent.
\(\beta_0\) is the intercept
\(\beta_1\) is the coefficient (or slope)
\(\epsilon\) represents the variation not explained by the model

In our case, the value of \(x\) (detected, the explanatory variable) - can only be TRUE or FALSE. It is usual in this case to assign FALSE a value of 0 and TRUE a value of 1.

If H. tumulorum is absent, \(x\) equals 0.
When \(x\) is zero, the line intercepts the y axis - so the intercept \(\beta_0\) is the mean minimum temperature when H. tumulorum is absent.
If H. tumulorum is present, \(x\) equals 1.
The slope is the change in \(y\) over one unit of \(x\). So, the change in mean minimum temperature between \(x\) = 0 and \(x\) = 1, or the difference in mean temperature when H. tumulorum is present, compared to when it is absent.

We know these numbers already:

gt(ht_temp_summ |> select(detected, mean))







detected
mean




FALSE
0.1128519


TRUE
1.3747955







The difference between the two means is:

diff <- pull(present, mean) - pull(absent, mean)
print(diff)

[1] 1.261944


When the bee is absent, \(x = 0\):
\[
y = 0.11 + (1.26 \times 0) + \epsilon
\]
so:
\[
y = 0.11 + \epsilon
\]
When the bee is present, \(x = 1\):
\[
y = 0.11 + (1.26 \times 1) + \epsilon
\]
so:
\[
y = 1.37 + \epsilon
\]
Our t-test tests whether there is evidence that the difference between the mean values of the two groups is different from zero.
Our linear model tests whether there is evidence that the slope of the line is different from zero.
They are therefore testing exactly the same thing.

Fitting linear models in R
Let’s see if this is correct by fitting a linear model to our data in R. We do this with the function lm() and the same formula we used previously - response ~ explanatory.
We can summarise the linear model using the function summary().

lm_ht <- lm(min_temp_coldest_month ~ detected,
  data = ht_temp_df
)
summ_lm_ht <- summary(lm_ht)
print(summ_lm_ht)


Call:
lm(formula = min_temp_coldest_month ~ detected, data = ht_temp_df)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-2.40085 -0.61417  0.02203  0.60461  2.55090 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    0.1129     0.1579   0.715    0.477    
detectedTRUE   1.2619     0.2204   5.726 2.07e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.9603 on 74 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.307, Adjusted R-squared:  0.2977 
F-statistic: 32.79 on 1 and 74 DF,  p-value: 2.073e-07


This function gives us a lot of information, including the numbers we calculated above.

The estimated intercept is our mean minimum temperature without H. tumulorum
The estimated slope (listed as detectedTRUE) is the difference in minimum temperature with and without H. tumulorum.
The p-value for the slope is identical to the p-value we calculated earlier with our t-test.

We can extract the 95% confidence intervals from our linear model with the function confint() with one argument - the fitted model.

ci <- confint(lm_ht)
print(ci)

                  2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept)  -0.2017249 0.4274287
detectedTRUE  0.8228055 1.7010818


The second confidence interval here is the confidence interval of the slope of the line - and again it’s identical to our t-test values above.
As discussed above, for a linear regression, we are interested in whether the coefficient (slope) for our explanatory variable differs from zero. We still use the t-statistic, which is calculated by dividing the estimated coefficient by its standard error.
The p-value is obtained from a t-distribution specified by the residual degrees of freedom. For a simple linear regression, we estimate two parameters: the intercept and the slope. Here we have 76 observations, so the residual degrees of freedom are 76 - 2 = 74.
We therefore need to look for the following values in the linear model output:

Coefficient (slope): Estimate
Test statistic: t value
Degrees of freedom: residual degrees of freedom
p-value: Pr(>|t|)
Proportion of variation explained: Multiple R-squared

For a linear model with a categorical explanatory variable like this, we can also report the difference in means between the two conditions.
For the linear model above, we could report:

There is evidence that minimum temperature differs according to the presence or absence of H. tumulorum (\(\beta\) = 1.26°C, 95% CI [0.82, 1.7]°C, \(t\)(74) = 5.73, \(p\) = 2.07e-07, \(R^2\) = 0.307). Sites where H. tumulorum is present have a mean minimum temperature approximately 1.26°C higher than sites where it is absent. The model explains approximately 30.7% of the variation in minimum temperature.



Visualising linear models in R
We can easily visualise our linear model in ggplot.
First, we plot a scatter plot with our detected variable on the x-axis and minimum temperature on the y-axis.
We need to convert our detected column to show 0 for FALSE and 1 for TRUE. To convert a column to numeric, we use the function as.numeric(). For a logical column, it will automatically do what we want - convert FALSE to 0 and TRUE to 1.
We can then use the function geom_smooth() to apply and plot a linear model to the data. This corresponds to plotting a line between 0.11 when x is 0 and 1.37 when x is 1.
Let’s also add a horizontal line using geom_hline() showing a slope of 0 and the same mean for both groups.

ht_temp_df <- ht_temp_df |>
  mutate(detected_num = as.numeric(detected))

overall_mean <- ht_temp_df |>
  pull(min_temp_coldest_month) |>
  mean()

ggplot(ht_temp_df, aes(
  x = detected_num,
  y = min_temp_coldest_month
)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = overall_mean), color = "red")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

title: Part 2: Hypothesis Testing
text:
ANOVA
With exactly two groups, a classical one-way ANOVA is also mathematically equivalent to either of these tests.
A one-way ANOVA with two groups is testing:
Does allowing the two groups to have different means explain significantly more variation than assuming they have the same mean
This can be simplified to - is there evidence that these two means are not equal?
This is asking the same question we’ve already asked twice, in a different way.
Let’s try an ANOVA. We run ANOVA in R on an existing linear model - which we already created above, using the function anova().

anova_lm <- anova(lm_ht)
anova_lm

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: min_temp_coldest_month
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
detected   1 30.237 30.2366  32.786 2.073e-07 ***
Residuals 74 68.245  0.9222                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


As you can see, we’ve again found an identical p-value. As it’s the same linear model, our confidence intervals are, by definition, also the same.
For an ANOVA, we report our results a little differently. The p-value here is obtained from an F distribution specified by two degrees-of-freedom values: the numerator and denominator degrees of freedom. The numerator degrees of freedom are associated with the explanatory variable. Here there are two groups (present and absent), so this is 2 − 1 = 1. The denominator degrees of freedom are the residual degrees of freedom. We have 76 observations and estimate two parameters (the intercept and slope), so this is 76 − 2 = 74.
As with the t-test, the p-value is calculated from a probability distribution. For ANOVA, this is the F-distribution rather than the t-distribution. The F-statistic compares the variation explained by the model with the unexplained variation; unusually large F-values provide evidence against the null hypothesis.
So, we need to look for the following values in our ANOVA output.

Test statistic: F value
Numerator degrees of freedom: Df for the explanatory variable
Denominator degrees of freedom: Df for the residuals
p-value: Pr(>F)







Figure 23.2: Interpreting ANOVA results



Additionally, we can report the proportion of variation explained by the model relative to the total variation in the response variable. We can calculate this from the sum of square values in the ANOVA output.

SS_model <- anova_lm["detected", "Sum Sq"]
SS_res <- anova_lm["Residuals", "Sum Sq"]

prop_var <- SS_model / (SS_res + SS_model)
print(prop_var)

[1] 0.3070276


Conveniently, this is the same as our \(R^2\) value in the linear model we used above.

print(summary(lm_ht))


Call:
lm(formula = min_temp_coldest_month ~ detected, data = ht_temp_df)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-2.40085 -0.61417  0.02203  0.60461  2.55090 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    0.1129     0.1579   0.715    0.477    
detectedTRUE   1.2619     0.2204   5.726 2.07e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.9603 on 74 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.307, Adjusted R-squared:  0.2977 
F-statistic: 32.79 on 1 and 74 DF,  p-value: 2.073e-07


So, we would report:

There is evidence that minimum temperature in the coldest month differs between sites where H. tumulorum is present and sites where it is absent (\(F\)(1, 74) = 32.79, \(p\) = 2.07e-07, \(R^2\) = 0.307). The model explains approximately 30.7% of the variation in minimum temperature in the coldest month.

The advantage of ANOVA is that, unlike a t-test, we can use it when our categorical explanatory variable has more than two groups - we’ll come to this in the next section.

title: Part 3: ANOVA
text:
One-way ANOVA with more than two groups
In the previous section, we used one-way ANOVA to look at the difference between two levels of a single explanatory variable. However, ANOVA can easily be expanded to look at multiple groups and multiple explanatory variables.
ANOVA expands easily to take into account an explanatory variable with more than two levels (i.e. a categorical variable with three or more options).
We already know about using response ~ explanatory as a formula in R to investigate response as a function of explanatory variable. If you are using a data frame as the input to this function and the explanatory variable is categorical, R will automatically treat the different values in the column as different levels of that variable.
One of the measurements in our pollinator data frame is mean_insect_mass - the mean mass in grams of all pollinators collected at that site.
It seems feasible that this would be affected by the types of pollinators present - some pollinators are much bigger than others.

title: Part 3: ANOVA
text:
Hypothesis
Using our pollinator data, let’s investigate the following hypothesis using a one-way ANOVA.

Null hypothesis: Sites dominated by different insect families have the same mean mass.
Alternative hypothesis: At least one dominant insect family is associated with sites with a different mean mass.

Let’s first list all the families which dominate at any site.

unique_fams <- site_metadata |> distinct(dominant_family)
print(unique_fams)

# A tibble: 4 × 1
  dominant_family
  <chr>          
1 Syrphidae      
2 Halictidae     
3 Apidae         
4 Andrenidae     


All sites are dominated by one of these four families.


Plot
A box plot is a typical way to visualise the type of data which is suitable for ANOVA analysis.

ggplot(
  site_metadata,
  aes(
    x = dominant_family, y = mean_insect_mass,
    fill = dominant_family
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw()










Statistical Test
We can test the association between mean insect mass and dominant family with a one-way ANOVA, and we define it exactly as before.
Here, we would define the linear model as lm(mean_insect_mass ~ dominant_family, data=site_metadata).
We could then just look at our linear model directly. It would take one category - in this case Andrenidae, as it is first alphabetically, to be the reference level and compare each of the other levels - Syrphidae, Halictidae and Apidae to Andrenidae. It would not compare e.g. Halictidae to Apidae as neither is the reference.
Let’s try it:

lm_mass_domfam <- lm(mean_insect_mass ~ dominant_family, data = site_metadata)
summary(lm_mass_domfam)


Call:
lm(formula = mean_insect_mass ~ dominant_family, data = site_metadata)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-17.5991  -5.3988  -0.5006   3.8201  20.9558 

Coefficients:
