title: Part 3: ANOVA
text:
Extension exercise - the F-distribution






Note



I stated above that “The p-value here is obtained from an F distribution specified by two degrees-of-freedom values: the numerator and denominator degrees of freedom. The numerator degrees of freedom are associated with the explanatory variable. The denominator degrees of freedom are the residual degrees of freedom.”. In this case, our numerator has three degrees of freedom and our denominator has 72.
In your pollinators.qmd Quarto file:

Simulate a sample of 1000 observations from F-distribution with 3 numerator degrees of freedom and 72 denominator degrees of freedom. You can draw a random sample from an F-distribution with the function rf with the arguments n - number of observations, df1 numerator degrees of freedom and df2 denominator degrees of freedom.
Create a dataframe where this set of observations forms a column.
Plot the results using the ggplot layer geom_density().
Calculate an approximate p-value using your simulated data — the proportion of simulated F-values which are greater than or equal to the F-statistic calculated from our data (14.72). You can extract the F-statistic from the ANOVA table using anova_mass_domfam["dominant_family", "F value"], changing anova_mass_domfam to whichever variable name you used.
Calculate the exact p-value using the F-distribution cumulative probability function pf().







AnswerAnswer






Simulate a sample of 1000 observations from F-distribution with 3 numerator degrees of freedom and 72 denominator degrees of freedom. You can draw a random sample from an F-distribution with the function rf with the arguments n - number of observations, df1 numerator degrees of freedom and df2 denominator degrees of freedom.

df_3_72 <- rf(1000, df1 = 3, df2 = 72)

Create a dataframe where this set of observations forms a column.

f_dist <- tibble(simulated = df_3_72)

Plot the results using the ggplot layer geom_density().

fstat <- anova_mass_domfam["dominant_family", "F value"]

ggplot(
  f_dist,
  aes(x = simulated)
) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = fstat, color = "red")








Calculate an approximate p-value using your simulated data — the proportion of simulated F-values which are greater than or equal to the F-statistic calculated from our data (14.72).

p_above_sim <- sum(f_dist$simulated >= fstat)

p_sim <- p_above_sim / nrow(f_dist)

print(p_sim)

[1] 0


As for the t-test previously, with 1000 simulations and such a low p-value, your value will almost certainly be zero.
Calculate the exact p-value using the F-distribution cumulative probability function pf().

p_below <- pf(fstat, 3, 72)
p_exact <- 1 - p_below
print(p_exact)

[1] 1.434646e-07


This should be the exact p-value calculated in our ANOVA.

title: Part 3: ANOVA
text:
Multi-way ANOVA
ANOVA can also be extended to include multiple categorical explanatory variables. This is called multi-way ANOVA (or factorial ANOVA). A model with two categorical explanatory variables is a two-way ANOVA, one with three is a three-way ANOVA, and so on.
We can add additional explanatory variables using + - response ~ explanatory1 + explanatory2 + explanatory3 etc.
The ANOVA tests whether each explanatory variable is associated with the response in turn. So, in the case above, explanatory1 would be tested first, followed by whether explanatory2 explains additional variation after explanatory1 has been included, and so forth.

Hypothesis
Using our pollinator data, let’s investigate the following hypotheses:
Dominant insect family:

Null hypothesis: mean insect mass is the same at sites dominated by different insect families
Alternative hypothesis: mean insect mass differs for at least one dominant insect family.

Broad habitat type:

Null hypothesis: after taking dominant insect family into account, mean insect mass is the same across different broad habitat types.
Alternative hypothesis: after taking dominant insect family into account, mean insect mass differs for at least one broad habitat type.



Plot
A box plot is again a typical visualisation to use here, this time using facet_wrap() to separate our different variables.

# Take the relevant columns from the data frame
domfam_habitat_sel <- site_metadata |>
  select(x1km_square, dominant_family, broad_habitat, mean_insect_mass)

# Pivot to long format
domfam_habitat_long <- domfam_habitat_sel |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(
      dominant_family,
      broad_habitat
    ),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  )

# Plot the boxplot
ggplot(
  domfam_habitat_long,
  aes(x = value, y = mean_insect_mass, fill = variable)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_x") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1)) # rotate x labels so they fit














ExerciseExercise 2






In your pollinators.qmd Quarto file:

Expand the linear model above to incorporate a second explanatory variable - broad habitat type (from the column broad_habitat) as well as dominant_family.
Run an ANOVA on the model and view the results.
Draw a conclusion based on your findings, including the appropriate statistical evidence to support your conclusion.







AnswerAnswer







Statistical Test
We define our linear model as follows:

lm_domfam_habitat_mass <- lm(mean_insect_mass ~ dominant_family + broad_habitat, data = site_metadata)

And then run the ANOVA.

anova_domfam_habitat_mass <- anova(lm_domfam_habitat_mass)
print(anova_domfam_habitat_mass)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: mean_insect_mass
                Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
dominant_family  3 3060.2 1020.06 14.6513 1.85e-07 ***
broad_habitat    4  255.5   63.87  0.9174    0.459    
Residuals       68 4734.3   69.62                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




Conclusion

There is evidence that mean insect mass differs among dominant insect families (\(F\)(3, 68) = 14.65, \(p\) = 1.85e-07). After accounting for dominant insect family, there is no evidence that broad habitat type explains additional variation in mean insect mass (\(F\)(4, 68) = 0.92, \(p\) = 0.46).

title: Part 3: ANOVA
text:
Interactions
When we use + to include multiple explanatory variables, we are assuming that their relationships with the response are additive. This means that the relationship between one explanatory variable and the response is the same at every level of the other explanatory variable. So for example, the dominant insect family can be associated with a difference in mean insect mass, and habitat can be associated with a difference, and these differences can be added together.
However, sometimes the relationship between one explanatory variable and the response depends on the value of another explanatory variable. This is called an interaction.
We can add interactions between variables using * - response ~ explanatory1 * explanatory2. The ANOVA will then test the association between each explanatory variable and the response, as well as whether there is an interaction between them.
For example, if we set up the model as mean_insect_mass ~ dominant_family * dominant_flower_order, we are asking:

Does mean insect mass vary between sites with different dominant insect families?
Does mean insect mass vary between sites with different dominant flower orders, once dominant insect family has been taken into account?
Does any difference in mean insect mass among dominant insect families depend on the dominant flower order?

This final question is the interaction: does the association between one explanatory variable and the response depend on the value of another explanatory variable?






ExerciseExercise 3






Let’s simulate a dataset with an interaction, to help illustrate this concept.
In this study, there are four populations of students and the response variable is the time they took to finish their lunch, in minutes. Response time is drawn from a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 3.
There are two categorical explanatory variables:

Did they use a spoon or a fork?
Did they eat soup or pasta?

Their mean finishing times are as follows:

Spoon + Pasta = 8 minutes
Fork + Pasta = 10 minutes
Spoon + Soup = 11 minutes
Fork + Soup = 25 minutes

The hypotheses here are:
Utensil:

Null: There is no association between utensil choice and finishing time.
Alternative: Utensil choice is associated with finishing time.

Food:

Null: There is no association between food choice and finishing time, after taking into account the association with utensil choice.
Alternative: Food choice is associated with finishing time, after taking into account the association with utensil choice.

Interaction:

Null: The association between utensil choice and finishing time does not vary depending on food choice.
Alternative: The association between utensil choice and finishing time varies depending on food choice.

In your prac4_exercises.qmd Quarto file:

Generate four simulated populations, each of 10 students, with response times normally distributed around these means and a standard deviation of 3.
Convert each of these into a data frame with the columns utensil, food and time.
Convert these to a single data frame using the function bind_rows(). You can pass any number of data frames as arguments to this function and it will return a single data frame combining all of the rows (assuming the data frames all have the same columns).
Fit a linear model with time as the response variable and utensil, food and their interaction as explanatory variables.
Run an ANOVA on the linear model.







AnswerAnswer







Data
Generate four simulated populations, each of 10 students, with response times normally distributed around these means and a standard deviation of 3.

spoon_pasta <- rnorm(10, 8, 3)
fork_pasta <- rnorm(10, 10, 3)
spoon_soup <- rnorm(10, 11, 3)
fork_soup <- rnorm(10, 25, 3)

Convert each of these into a data frame with the columns utensil, food and time.

df_sp <- tibble(
  utensil = "Spoon",
  food = "Pasta",
  time = spoon_pasta
)

df_fp <- tibble(
  utensil = "Fork",
  food = "Pasta",
  time = fork_pasta
)

df_ss <- tibble(
  utensil = "Spoon",
  food = "Soup",
  time = spoon_soup
)

df_fs <- tibble(
  utensil = "Fork",
  food = "Soup",
  time = fork_soup
)

Convert these to a single data frame using the function bind_rows(). You can pass any number of data frames as arguments to this function and it will return a single data frame combining all of the rows (assuming the data frames all have the same columns).

df_food <- bind_rows(df_sp, df_fp, df_ss, df_fs)



Statistical test
Fit a linear model with time as the response variable and utensil, food and their interaction as explanatory variables.

lm_lunch <- lm(time ~ utensil * food, data = df_food)

Run an ANOVA on the linear model.

anova_lunch <- anova(lm_lunch)
print(anova_lunch)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: time
             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
utensil       1 580.00  580.00  51.270 2.025e-08 ***
food          1 755.45  755.45  66.779 1.018e-09 ***
utensil:food  1 405.33  405.33  35.830 7.259e-07 ***
Residuals    36 407.25   11.31                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1








Conclusion
Here, we need to report the F-statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value for both explanatory variables and for the interaction.

There is evidence that eating time differs according to the utensil used (\(F\)(1, 36) = 51.27, \(p\) = 2.03e-08) and according to the type of food being eaten (\(F\)(1, 36) = 66.78, \(p\) = 1.02e-09).
There is also evidence of an interaction between utensil and food (\(F\)(1, 36) = 35.83, \(p\) = 7.26e-07). This means that the difference in eating time between using a fork and a spoon depends on the type of food being eaten.







NoteBonus Exercise: Removing the interaction



Change the population means so that there is no interaction between food and utensil, but both food and utensil are still associated with eating time, then re-run the ANOVA and re-interpret the results.






AnswerAnswer






For example

# Simulate the populations
spoon_pasta <- rnorm(10, 8, 3)
fork_pasta <- rnorm(10, 12, 3)
spoon_soup <- rnorm(10, 14, 3)
fork_soup <- rnorm(10, 18, 3)

# Make the data frames
df_sp <- tibble(
  utensil = "Spoon",
  food = "Pasta",
  time = spoon_pasta
)

df_fp <- tibble(
  utensil = "Fork",
  food = "Pasta",
  time = fork_pasta
)

df_ss <- tibble(
  utensil = "Spoon",
  food = "Soup",
  time = spoon_soup
)

df_fs <- tibble(
  utensil = "Fork",
  food = "Soup",
  time = fork_soup
)

# Combine the data frames
df_food <- bind_rows(df_sp, df_fp, df_ss, df_fs)


Statistical Test

# Fit the linear model
lm_lunch <- lm(time ~ utensil * food, data = df_food)

# Run the ANOVA
anova_lunch <- anova(lm_lunch)
print(anova_lunch)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: time
             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
utensil       1 183.16  183.16 26.1797 1.052e-05 ***
food          1 468.43  468.43 66.9523 9.869e-10 ***
utensil:food  1  38.76   38.76  5.5395   0.02417 *  
Residuals    36 251.87    7.00                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




Conclusion

There is evidence that eating time differs according to the utensil used (\(F\)(1, 36) = 26.18, \(p\) = 1.05e-05) and according to the type of food being eaten (\(F\)(1, 36) = 66.95, \(p\) = 9.87e-10).
However, there is no evidence of an interaction between utensil and food (\(F\)(1, 36) = 5.54, \(p\) = 0.0242). This means there is no evidence that the difference in eating time between using a fork and a spoon depends on the type of food being eaten.














Hypotheses
Now, let’s try this with our real data. Here, our hypotheses are:
Dominant insect family:

Null: There is no association between mean insect mass and dominant insect family.
Alternative: Mean insect mass is associated with dominant insect family.

Dominant flower order:

Null: There is no association between mean insect mass and dominant flower order, once dominant insect family has been taken into account.
Alternative: Mean insect mass is associated with dominant flower order, once dominant insect family has been taken into account.

Interaction:

Null: The association between dominant insect family and mean insect mass does not vary depending on dominant flower order.
Alternative: The association between dominant insect family and mean insect mass varies depending on dominant flower order.

title: Part 4: Linear regression and Chi-Squared
text:
Linear Regression
We’ve now used all sorts of linear models, but how about a standard linear regression between two continuous variables? You already have the skills needed to do this - you can fit the model using lm() and then view the results using summary(), and you basically know how to interpret the results.
As we discussed in the previous section, for a linear model we should report the following:
For a linear regression with two continuous variables, we can also report the amount the mean of the response variable changes when the explanatory variable changes by one unit.
Let’s use the pollinator data again and look at a straightforward regression question - how is total annual precipitation (column annual_total_prec) associated with mean annual temperature (column annual_mean_temp)?
crumbs: 25  Part 4: Linear regression and Chi-Squared

title: Part 4: Linear regression and Chi-Squared
text:
Coefficient (slope): Estimate – the expected change in the response variable associated with a one-unit increase in that explanatory variable, holding the other explanatory variables constant.
Test statistic: t value
Degrees of freedom: residual degrees of freedom
p-value: Pr(>|t|)
Proportion of variation explained: Multiple R-squared




Hypotheses

Null: There is no association between total annual precipitation and mean annual temperature.
Alternative: Total annual precipitation is associated with mean annual temperature.



Plot
A scatter plot is the most common plot to compare two continuous variables. We can use geom_smooth(method = "lm") to add a linear model to the plot.

ggplot(site_metadata,
       aes(x = annual_mean_temp,
           y = annual_total_prec)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
crumbs: 25  Part 4: Linear regression and Chi-Squared

title: Part 4: Linear regression and Chi-Squared
text:
Multiple linear regression
Just as we included multiple explanatory variables in our ANOVA, we can include multiple continuous explanatory variables in a linear regression. This is called multiple linear regression. We can also add interaction terms.
For example, we could ask if precipitation is associated with temperature, elevation or the interaction between the two, using annual_total_prec ~ annual_mean_temp * elevation.
There is one complication here - by default, a multiple regression containing an interaction will determine the association with each explanatory variable when the value of the other explanatory variables is zero. This is not the case for an additive model, where the association with each explanatory variable is estimated while holding the other explanatory variables constant.
So, in our case, our model annual_total_prec ~ annual_mean_temp * elevation will tell us:

Is precipitation associated with annual mean temperature when elevation is 0?
Is precipitation associated with elevation when annual mean temperature is 0?
Does the association between annual mean temperature and precipitation depend on elevation?

The first two questions are not usually quite what we want to ask. Better questions might be:

Is precipitation associated with annual mean temperature at the mean elevation.
Is precipitation associated with elevation at the mean annual temperature.

We can ask this by centring our data for elevation and temperature - subtracting our mean value from all observations to create a new set of centred observations with mean zero. The shape and spread of the variables remains the same, but the model is now answering more useful questions.
Let’s add these new columns to our data frame.

site_metadata_cent <- site_metadata |>
  mutate(
    annual_mean_temp_cent = annual_mean_temp - mean(annual_mean_temp),
    elevation_cent = elevation - mean(elevation)
  )


Hypotheses
So, now our hypotheses are:
Annual mean temperature:

Null: At the mean elevation, there is no association between annual mean temperature and precipitation.
Alternative: At the mean elevation, there is an association between annual mean temperature and precipitation.

Elevation:

Null: At the mean annual temperature, there is no association between elevation and precipitation.
Alternative: At the mean annual temperature, there is an association between elevation and precipitation.

Interaction:

Null: The association between annual mean temperature and precipitation does not depend on elevation.
Alternative: The association between annual mean temperature and precipitation depends on elevation.



Plot
A scatter plot is again a good visualisation here, and we can use the function facet_wrap() again to separate the data into two plots, one for annual mean temperature vs annual total precipitation, and one for elevation vs annual total precipitation.

# Extract relevant columns and convert to long format
elev_temp_long <- site_metadata |>
  select(x1km_square, annual_total_prec,
         annual_mean_temp, elevation) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(
      annual_mean_temp,
      elevation
    ),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  )

# Plot
ggplot(elev_temp_long,
       aes(x = value,
           y = annual_total_prec)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scale='free_x') +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Statistical test
Now we can fit our linear model using these new columns.

lm_elev_temp <- lm(annual_total_prec ~ annual_mean_temp_cent * elevation_cent, data = site_metadata_cent)
summ_lm_elev_temp <- summary(lm_elev_temp)
print(summ_lm_elev_temp)


Call:
lm(formula = annual_total_prec ~ annual_mean_temp_cent * elevation_cent, 
    data = site_metadata_cent)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-517.10 -186.68  -77.44  189.05  637.89 

Coefficients:
                                      Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)                          1075.9594    36.3408  29.608  < 2e-16 ***
annual_mean_temp_cent                 -66.3939    42.4250  -1.565 0.121975    
elevation_cent                          1.6579     0.4555   3.639 0.000511 ***
annual_mean_temp_cent:elevation_cent    0.0771     0.1657   0.465 0.643064

Conclusion

There is no evidence of an association between mean annual temperature and total annual precipitation at the mean elevation (\(b\) = -66.39, \(t\)(72) = -1.56, \(p\) = 0.122). There is evidence of a positive association between elevation and total annual precipitation at the mean annual temperature (\(b\) = 1.66, \(t\)(72) = 3.64, \(p\) = 5.11e-04). There is no evidence of an interaction between mean annual temperature and elevation (\(b\) = 0.077, \(t\)(72) = 0.47, \(p\) = 0.643), so there is no evidence that the association between temperature and precipitation changes with elevation. Overall, the model explains 53.3% of the variation in total annual precipitation (\(R^2\) = 0.533).
crumbs: 25  Part 4: Linear regression and Chi-Squared

title: Part 4: Linear regression and Chi-Squared
text:
Multicollinearity
This result seems strange at first — precipitation was strongly associated with annual mean temperature when temperature was the only explanatory variable, but there is no longer strong evidence for that association once elevation is included.
Multicollinearity occurs when two or more explanatory variables in a multiple regression are strongly associated with each other.
For example, we are trying to explain variation in precipitation using both temperature and elevation. But if elevation and temperature are closely related - for example, if higher sites tend to be colder - the model is trying to separate the associations with two variables which tend to change together.

If only temperature is in the model, we are asking - does temperature explain variation in precipitation?
If both temperature and elevation are in the model, we are asking - does temperature explain variation in precipitation over and above the variation associated with elevation?

If temperature and elevation are highly correlated, there may not be much independent information with which to separate their associations with precipitation. Consequently, the estimated individual coefficients can become less precise, their standard errors can become larger, and their p-values can increase.
This does not necessarily mean that the multiple regression model is worse at explaining precipitation. Rather, multicollinearity makes it more difficult to determine the individual association between each explanatory variable and the response.
Let’s check the correlation between the annual mean temperature and elevation. We can calculate the correlation coefficient using the R function cor·

correlation <- site_metadata |>
  summarise(correlation = cor(annual_mean_temp, elevation))

gt(correlation)







correlation




-0.817405







We can also visualise this:

ggplot(site_metadata, 
       aes(x = annual_mean_temp, y = elevation)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









These two variables are clearly highly correlated (\(r\) = `r round(correlation, 2)), so multicollinearity is a plausible explanation for the much higher p-value for temperature when elevation is included in the model.






NoteBonus content: Investigating multicollinearity





We can investigate the effect of multicollinearity by explicitly controlling the correlation between our explanatory variables.
Since at this point in the practical I think we need a picture of a hedgehog, let’s say we want to predict if the weight of a hedgehog in grams is associated with:

How much water it drinks per day in millilitres.
How much food it eats per day in grams.







Figure 25.1: A hedgehog eating



Let’s say that:

For each 100 ml of water the hedgehog drinks per day, its weight is 30 g heavier on average.
For each 100 g of food the hedgehog eats per day, its weight is 50 g heavier on average.
The effects are additive with no interaction.

\[
\text{weight}_i = 500 + 0.3\,\text{water}_i + 0.5\,\text{food}_i + \epsilon_i
\]
Let’s say we have 50 hedgehogs, and hedgehog water intake is a normal distribution with mean 70 ml and standard deviation 40 ml. There is also random noise with a mean of 0g and a standard deviation of 30 g.

n_hedgehogs <- 50
water <- rnorm(n_hedgehogs, 70, 40)
noise <- rnorm(n_hedgehogs, 0, 30)

To investigate multicollinearity, we will simulate food and water consumption with different strengths of association - i.e. with different values of \(R^2\) - between food and water intake.
We can do this by constructing food consumption with a proportion of variation associated with water consumption and a proportion of random variation. As we increase the extent to which food consumption is associated with water consumption, \(R^2\) between the two explanatory variables increases.
Importantly, we will not change the relationship between food, water and hedgehog weight. This allows us to investigate what happens to our regression estimates as multicollinearity increases.
First, we centre and scale the variation in water consumption so it has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. We can also generate random noise with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

water_z <- (water - mean(water)) / sd(water)
noise_food <- rnorm(n_hedgehogs, 0, 1)

Here, \(R^2\) is the squared correlation between food and water intake, and describes the proportion of variation in food intake associated with variation in water intake.
For example, to simulate \(R^2\) = 0.3, we construct food intake so that 30% of its variance comes from the component associated with water intake and 70% comes from random variation.

rsq <- 0.3

food_var_water <- sqrt(rsq) * water_z
food_var_noise <- sqrt(1 - rsq) * noise_food

food_var_total <- food_var_water + food_var_noise

We can then scale these standardised values so that food intake has a mean of 100 g per day and a standard deviation of 50 g.

mean_food <- 100
food_sd <- 50
food <- mean_food + (food_var_total * food_sd)

This gives us 50 food data points which have a mean of approx 100g, a standard deviation of approx 50g and an \(R^2\) of approx 0.3 with water intake.

print(paste("mean = ", mean(food)))

[1] "mean =  92.0929749689055"

print(paste("sd = ", sd(food)))

[1] "sd =  55.2113355374634"

print(paste("R2 = ", cor(food, water)^2))

[1] "R2 =  0.331159596417852"


Now we can run this analysis with \(R^2\) values ranging from 0 to 0.99, with an increment of 0.01.

hog_results <- tibble()

for (rsq in seq(0, 0.99, 0.01)) {
  # Calculate the food values based on the water values
  # plus noise
  food_var_water <- sqrt(rsq) * water_z
  food_var_noise <- sqrt(1 - rsq) * noise_food
  food_var_total <- food_var_water + food_var_noise

  # Scale up food values
  food <- mean_food + (food_var_total * food_sd)

  # Apply the model to calculate hedgehog weight
  hogs <- 500 + (water * 0.3) + (food * 0.5) + noise

  # Put the three columns into a data frame
  hog_df <- tibble(
    weight = hogs,
    water = water,
    food = food
  )

  # Fit and summarise the linear model
  lm_hogs_both <- summary(lm(weight ~ water + food, data = hog_df))

  # Store the results of the lm
  hog_results <- bind_rows(
    hog_results,
    tibble(
      rsq = rsq,
      observed_rsq = cor(water, food)^2,
      water_estimate = lm_hogs_both$coefficients["water", "Estimate"],
      water_se = lm_hogs_both$coefficients["water", "Std. Error"],
      water_p = lm_hogs_both$coefficients["water", "Pr(>|t|)"],
      food_estimate = lm_hogs_both$coefficients["food", "Estimate"],
      food_se = lm_hogs_both$coefficients["food", "Std. Error"],
      food_p = lm_hogs_both$coefficients["food", "Pr(>|t|)"],
      model_rsq = lm_hogs_both$r.squared
    )
  )
}

Now we can convert the data frame to long format, to make plotting easier.

hog_results_long <- hog_results |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      water_estimate, water_se, water_p,
      food_estimate, food_se, food_p
    ),
    names_to = c("predictor", "statistic"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_to = "value"
  )

We can then plot the following at each \(R^2\):

The estimate - the estimated slope for each explanatory variable: the expected change in the response variable associated with a one-unit increase in that explanatory variable, holding the other explanatory variables constant.
The p-value
The standard error


ggplot(hog_results_long, aes(x = rsq, y = value, color = predictor)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~statistic, scale = "free_y") +
  theme_bw()








It is very clear from these plots that at high values of (R^2), the coefficient estimates become less stable and their standard errors increase. As a result, the test statistics tend to become smaller and the p-values larger, making it more difficult to detect the individual associations of food and water intake with hedgehog weight.
This doesn’t mean the model is useless, and we can see this if we plot the model \(R^2\) - the total proportion of variance explained by the model.

ggplot(hog_results, aes(x = rsq, y = model_rsq)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  theme_bw()








Even when the explanatory variables are highly correlated, the model as a whole can still explain a large proportion of the variation in hedgehog weight. Multicollinearity mainly makes it difficult to estimate and interpret the individual coefficients reliably.

title: Part 4: Linear regression and Chi-Squared
text:
Chi-squared
Chi-squared looks for an association between two categorical variables. Unlike all the other tests we’ve covered so far, it is not based on a linear model.
For a chi-squared we typically report: * \(X^2\) test statistic * Degrees of freedom * p-value

Hypotheses
In our pollinator data set, let’s investigate the following hypothesis:

Alternative: There is an association between land cover (agricultural or semi-natural, all of our sites are in one of these two categories) and UK country (England, Scotland or Wales, this dataset doesn’t cover Northern Ireland) amongst the sites in the POMS dataset.
Null: There is no association between land cover and UK country amongst the sites in the POMS dataset.



Plot
For chi-squared, we need to count the number of observations with each combination of variables. We can do this using the count() function.

country_habitat_counts <- site_metadata |>
  count(land_cover, country)

gt(country_habitat_counts)







land_cover
country
n




agricultural
England
30


agricultural
Scotland
6


agricultural
Wales
9


semi-natural
England
6


semi-natural
Scotland
17


semi-natural
Wales
8







A useful visualisation is a stacked bar chart, where the y axis is count, and each bar represents one categorial variable and has different coloured sections representing the other categorical variable.

ggplot(country_habitat_counts,
       aes(x = country, y = n, fill=land_cover)) +
  geom_col()










Contingency table
The input for the chisq.test() function is a contingency table, showing the number of observations with each combination of categories.




agricultural
semi-natural






England
count
count




Scotland
count
count




Wales
count
count





We already know how to generate these counts - we have them above - but the chisq.test() function is a little picky about the input, so instead we will use another function, xtabs(), which is specifically made to use to create contingency tables.
xtabs() uses the same formula syntax as many R stats functions, as follows:

cont_table_country_habitat <- xtabs(
  ~ country + land_cover,
  data = site_metadata
)
print(cont_table_country_habitat)

          land_cover
country    agricultural semi-natural
  England            30            6
  Scotland            6           17
  Wales               9            8




Statistical test
Now we can run the chi-squared test.

chisq_country_habitat <- chisq.test(cont_table_country_habitat)
print(chisq_country_habitat)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  cont_table_country_habitat
X-squared = 19.399, df = 2, p-value = 6.131e-05


There was strong evidence of an association between country and habitat type (\(\chi^2\)(2) = 19.40, \(p\) = 6.13 × 10-5).
With the chi-squared test, we can also see the expected counts for each category - the counts we would expect if the null hypothesis were true.

print(chisq_country_habitat$expected)

          land_cover
country    agricultural semi-natural
  England      21.31579    14.684211
  Scotland     13.61842     9.381579
  Wales        10.06579     6.934211


The chi-squared test compares these expected counts with our observed counts. The greater the differences between the observed and expected counts, the greater the evidence against the null hypothesis.

title: Part 5: Hypothesis Testing Exercises
text:
Statistical test recap
Here is a reminder of some statistical tests and the data types they are appropriate for.
As long as there are many possible values (e.g. the values aren’t limited to 1, 2 or 3), count data (such as number of insects) can be treated as continuous when used as an explanatory variable. For the tests in this table, response variables described as continuous should usually be genuinely continuous rather than counts.

title: Part 5: Hypothesis Testing Exercises
text:
Hypothesis testing exercises
Now we are ready to test some hypotheses based on the POMS data.






ExerciseExercise 1






In your pollinators.qmd Quarto file, using the appropriate statistical tests, investigate at least three of the following questions. Try to choose questions requiring different tests.
For each hypothesis, choose an appropriate statistical test and visualisation (a box plot, bar chart or scatter plot). Interpret the result using the relevant test statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value. Where relevant to the test used, also consider the confidence interval, effect size and proportion of variation explained by the model.
For this exercise, assume that the underlying assumptions of the appropriate model have been met — you do not need to check or plot these. There is also no need to plot maps.
The data you need are in the site_metadata data frame unless otherwise specified.

Different countries in the UK are quite diverse in terms of habitat and climate. Test the hypothesis that country (Scotland, England or Wales; column country) is associated with whether sites are dominated by bees (family Apidae) or hoverflies (family Syrphidae) (column dominant_family, you will need to filter to include only these families).







AnswerAnswer






Count the groups for the plot.

sites_apidae_syrphidae <- site_metadata |>
  filter(dominant_family %in% c("Apidae", "Syrphidae"))
country_family_counts <- sites_apidae_syrphidae |>
  count(country, dominant_family)

Plot a bar chart of the data.

ggplot(country_family_counts, aes(x = country, y = n, fill = dominant_family)) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_bw()








Make a contingency table.

cont_table <- xtabs(
  ~ country + dominant_family,
  data = sites_apidae_syrphidae
)
print(cont_table)

          dominant_family
country    Apidae Syrphidae
  England      20         8
  Scotland      7        15
  Wales         7        10


Perform a chi-squared test.

cs <- chisq.test(cont_table)
print(cs)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  cont_table
X-squared = 8.5683, df = 2, p-value = 0.01379


There is evidence of an association between dominant insect family (Apidae vs Syrphidae) and country (\(\chi^2\)(2) = 8.57, \(p\) = 0.0138). Sites in Scotland and Wales were observed to be more frequently dominated by Syrphidae, whereas sites in England were more frequently dominated by Apidae.





Very broadly, increased biomass is thought to be associated with higher temperatures and higher precipitation. Test the hypothesis that total insect biomass (column total_insect_biomass) is associated with annual mean temperature (annual_mean_temp) and annual total precipitation (annual_total_prec), with an additive effect, at these UK sites. Does the direction of each estimated relationship agree with the hypothesis?







AnswerAnswer






Convert the data to long format.

biomass_tp <- site_metadata |>
  select(total_insect_biomass, annual_mean_temp, annual_total_prec) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(annual_mean_temp, annual_total_prec),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "measurement"
  )

Plot the relationship between insect biomass and each explanatory variable.

ggplot(biomass_tp, aes(
  x = measurement,
  y = total_insect_biomass
)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_x") +
  theme_bw()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









Perform a multiple linear regression.

lm_biomass_tp <- lm(total_insect_biomass ~ annual_mean_temp + annual_total_prec, data = site_metadata)
lm_biomass_tp_summary <- summary(lm_biomass_tp)
print(lm_biomass_tp_summary)


Call:
lm(formula = total_insect_biomass ~ annual_mean_temp + annual_total_prec, 
    data = site_metadata)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
 -7253  -2897  -1172   1599  20796 

Coefficients:
                   Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)  
(Intercept)       16153.044   7780.387   2.076   0.0414 *
annual_mean_temp   -672.935    682.706  -0.986   0.3275  
annual_total_prec    -3.508      2.252  -1.558   0.1237  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5444 on 73 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.03221,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.005692 
F-statistic: 1.215 on 2 and 73 DF,  p-value: 0.3027


There is no evidence that total insect biomass is associated with annual mean temperature and annual total precipitation in this model (\(F\)(2, 73) = 1.21, p=0.3027). The model explained only 3.2% of the variation in total insect biomass (\(R^2\) = 0.0322). There was no evidence of an association with either annual mean temperature (coefficient = -672.94, p=0.3275) or annual total precipitation (coefficient = -3.51, p=0.1237), after accounting for the other variable. Both estimated relationships were negative, which is opposite to the direction predicted by our hypothesis.





Sites at higher elevation may be subject to greater temperature variation than sites at lower elevation. Test the hypothesis that elevation (elevation) is associated with annual temperature range (temp_annual_range). Does the direction of the estimated relationship agree with the hypothesis?







AnswerAnswer






Plot a scatter plot of the two variables.

ggplot(
  site_metadata,
  aes(x = elevation, y = temp_annual_range)
) +
  geom_point()








Perform a linear regression.

temp_elev <- lm(temp_annual_range ~ elevation, data = site_metadata)
temp_elev_summ <- summary(temp_elev)
print(temp_elev_summ)


Call:
lm(formula = temp_annual_range ~ elevation, data = site_metadata)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-4.0420 -0.9127  0.2317  1.1983  2.2673 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 18.813762   0.297097  63.325   <2e-16 ***
elevation   -0.002533   0.001376  -1.841   0.0697 .  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.519 on 74 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.04378,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.03086 
F-statistic: 3.388 on 1 and 74 DF,  p-value: 0.06968


There is no evidence of an association between elevation and annual temperature range at these sites (coefficient = -0.0025, \(t\)(74) = -1.84, \(p\) = 0.0697, \(R^2\) = 0.0438). The estimated relationship is negative, which is opposite to the direction predicted by our hypothesis.





Melanostoma scalare, the chequered hoverfly, can be associated with sand dunes and undercliffs. Test the hypothesis that sites where M. scalare is present (you will need to create this column from the insect counts data frame and join it to the site metadata data frame) have a different mean distance from the coast (column distance_to_coast) from sites where it is absent. Does the direction of the observed difference agree with the biological prediction?







AnswerAnswer






Add a column showing the presence or absence of M. scalare to the site metadata data frame.

ms_present <- insect_counts |>
  filter(species == "Melanostoma scalare") |>
  mutate(detected = n_observed > 0) |>
  left_join(site_metadata)

Joining with `by = join_by(x1km_square)`


Plot the distribution of distance from the coast according to the presence or absence of M. scalare.

ggplot(
  ms_present,
  aes(
    x = detected,
    y = distance_to_coast,
    fill = detected
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw()








Perform a t-test.

ms_coast_test <- t.test(
  distance_to_coast ~ detected,
  data = ms_present,
  var.equal = TRUE
)

print(ms_coast_test)


    Two Sample t-test

data:  distance_to_coast by detected
t = -3.0162, df = 74, p-value = 0.003507
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group FALSE and group TRUE is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -32.108294  -6.562073
sample estimates:
mean in group FALSE  mean in group TRUE 
           25.84124            45.17642 



ms_t <- round(ms_coast_test$statistic, 2)
ms_df <- round(ms_coast_test$parameter)
ms_p <- round(ms_coast_test$p.value, 4)

ms_ci_lower <- round(ms_coast_test$conf.int[1], 2)
ms_ci_upper <- round(ms_coast_test$conf.int[2], 2)

ms_mean_absent <- round(ms_coast_test$estimate[1], 2)
ms_mean_present <- round(ms_coast_test$estimate[2], 2)

There is evidence that mean distance from the coast differs between sites where M. scalare is present and sites where it is absent (\(t\)(74) = -3.02, \(p\) = 0.0035, 95% CI [-32.11, -6.56] km). Mean distance from the coast was 45.18 km at sites where M. scalare was present, compared with 25.84 km where it was absent. The direction of the observed difference therefore does not agree with the biological prediction: M. scalare was found at sites that were, on average, further from the coast.





Buff-tailed bumblebees, Bombus terrestris, are big. Test the hypothesis that total insect biomass (column total_insect_biomass) differs according to presence/absence of B. terrestris (you will need to create this column based on the insect counts data frame).







AnswerAnswer






Add a column showing the presence or absence of B. terrestris to the site metadata data frame.

bumblebees <- insect_counts |>
  filter(species == "Bombus terrestris") |>
  mutate(detected = n_observed > 0) |>
  left_join(site_metadata)

Joining with `by = join_by(x1km_square)`


Plot the total insect biomass according to the presence or absence of B. terrestris.

ggplot(
  bumblebees,
  aes(
    x = detected,
    y = total_insect_biomass,
    fill = detected
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw()








Perform a t-test.

big_bee_test <- t.test(
  total_insect_biomass ~ detected,
  data = bumblebees,
  var.equal = TRUE
)

print(big_bee_test)


    Two Sample t-test

data:  total_insect_biomass by detected
t = -4.1495, df = 74, p-value = 8.801e-05
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group FALSE and group TRUE is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -8203.273 -2880.850
sample estimates:
mean in group FALSE  mean in group TRUE 
           2311.674            7853.736 



bb_t <- round(big_bee_test$statistic, 2)
bb_df <- round(big_bee_test$parameter)
bb_p <- big_bee_test$p.value

bb_ci_lower <- round(big_bee_test$conf.int[1], 2)
bb_ci_upper <- round(big_bee_test$conf.int[2], 2)

bb_mean_absent <- round(big_bee_test$estimate[1], 2)
bb_mean_present <- round(big_bee_test$estimate[2], 2)

There is evidence that the total insect biomass differs between sites where B. terrestris is present and sites where it is absent (\(t\)(74) = -4.15, \(p\) = 0.0001, 95% CI [-8203.27, -2880.85] g). Mean total insect biomass was 7853.74 g at sites where B. terrestris was present, compared with 2311.67 g where it was absent. The direction of the observed difference therefore agrees with the biological prediction: B. terrestris was found at sites with, on average, higher total insect biomass.





The heath bumblebee Bombus jonellus is named because it likes heathland, and heathland is often dominated by the plant heather, Calluna vulgaris. Test the hypothesis that the presence of B. jonellus (you will need to create this column based on the insect counts data frame) is associated with the presence of C.vulgaris (you will need to create this column based on the flower counts data frame).







AnswerAnswer






Count the groups for the plot.

heath_df <- insect_counts |>
  filter(species == "Bombus jonellus") |>
  mutate(bees_detected = n_observed > 0) |>
  left_join(site_metadata)

Joining with `by = join_by(x1km_square)`

heath_df <- flower_counts |>
  filter(flower_species == "Calluna vulgaris") |>
  mutate(heather_detected = n_observed_flowers > 0) |>
  left_join(heath_df)

Joining with `by = join_by(x1km_square)`

heath_counts <- heath_df |>
  count(bees_detected, heather_detected)

Plot a bar chart of the data.

ggplot(heath_counts, aes(x = bees_detected, y = n, fill = heather_detected)) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_bw()








Make a contingency table.

cont_table <- xtabs(
  ~ bees_detected + heather_detected,
  data = heath_df
)
print(cont_table)

             heather_detected
bees_detected FALSE TRUE
        FALSE    50   10
        TRUE      6   10


Perform a chi-squared test.

cs <- chisq.test(cont_table)

Warning in chisq.test(cont_table): Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect

print(cs)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  cont_table
X-squared = 11.423, df = 1, p-value = 0.0007254


There is evidence of an association between the presence of the heath bumblebee B. jonellus and of heather C. vulgaris (\(\chi^2\)(1) = 11.42, \(p\) = 0.0007). Sites in which B. jonellus is present more frequently have C. vulgaris present.
Note: there are technically not quite enough values here for a chi-squared test, so you may see a warning. For the purposes of this exercise, don’t worry about it.





Environmental conditions and the diversity of available floral resources may influence the types of insects supported at a site. Test the hypothesis that mean insect mass (column mean_insect_mass) is associated with flower biodiversity (column n_unique_flowers), annual mean temperature (column annual_mean_temp), or an interaction between these two variables.







AnswerAnswer






Centre the explanatory variables.

centered_site_md <- site_metadata |>
  mutate(
    centered_annual_mean_temp = annual_mean_temp -
      mean(annual_mean_temp),
    centered_n_unique_flowers = n_unique_flowers -
      mean(n_unique_flowers)
  )

Convert the data to long format.

biomass_biodiv_temp <- centered_site_md |>
  select(
    mean_insect_mass,
    centered_annual_mean_temp,
    centered_n_unique_flowers
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(
      centered_annual_mean_temp,
      centered_n_unique_flowers
    ),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "measurement"
  )

Plot the relationship between mean insect mass and each explanatory variable.

ggplot(biomass_biodiv_temp, aes(
  x = measurement,
  y = mean_insect_mass
)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_x") +
  theme_bw()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









Perform a multiple linear regression.

lm_mass_biodiv_temp <- lm(mean_insect_mass ~ centered_annual_mean_temp * centered_n_unique_flowers, data = centered_site_md)
lm_mass_biodiv_temp_summary <- summary(lm_mass_biodiv_temp)
print(lm_mass_biodiv_temp_summary)


Call:
lm(formula = mean_insect_mass ~ centered_annual_mean_temp * centered_n_unique_flowers, 
    data = centered_site_md)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-21.129  -5.901  -1.003   4.990  25.509 

Coefficients:
                                                    Estimate Std. Error t value
(Intercept)                                         27.96091    1.36364  20.505
centered_annual_mean_temp                           -0.82033    1.21463  -0.675
centered_n_unique_flowers                           -0.26172    0.11786  -2.221
centered_annual_mean_temp:centered_n_unique_flowers  0.12281    0.09203   1.334
                                                    Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)                                           <2e-16 ***
centered_annual_mean_temp                             0.5016    
centered_n_unique_flowers                             0.0295 *  
centered_annual_mean_temp:centered_n_unique_flowers   0.1863    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 9.686 on 72 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1608,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1258 
F-statistic: 4.599 on 3 and 72 DF,  p-value: 0.005313


There is evidence that the overall model is associated with mean insect mass (\(F\)(3, 72) = 4.6, \(p\) = 0.0053, \(R^2\) = 0.161), with the model explaining 16.1% of the variation in mean insect mass.
At the average annual mean temperature, there is evidence of an association between flower diversity and mean insect mass (coefficient = -0.26, \(p\) = 0.0295). The estimated coefficient is negative, indicating that sites with greater flower diversity tend to have lower mean insect mass.
At the average level of flower diversity, there is no evidence of an association between annual mean temperature and mean insect mass (coefficient = -0.82, \(p\) = 0.5016).
There is also no evidence of an interaction between annual mean temperature and flower diversity (interaction coefficient = 0.12, \(p\) = 0.1863). Therefore, there is no evidence that the relationship between flower diversity and mean insect mass changes with annual mean temperature.





Bramble plants, particularly the blackberry plant Rubus fruticosus, are considered to be one of the major food sources for bees (family Apidae). Test the hypothesis that mean insect mass (column mean_insect_mass) differs according to the presence/absence of R. fruticosus (you will need to create this column from the flower counts data frame) and the dominant pollinator family (column dominant_family) or the interaction between these two variables.

Note: If you want to use facet_wrap to plot both dominant_family and presence/absence of R. fruticosus with the same ggplot() function, you will need to convert your presence/absence column from logical to character type using the function as.character() before converting your data frame to long format.






AnswerAnswer






Add a column showing the presence or absence of R. fruticosus to the site metadata data frame.

blackberries <- flower_counts |>
  filter(flower_species == "Rubus fruticosus") |>
  mutate(detected = n_observed_flowers > 0) |>
  left_join(site_metadata)

Joining with `by = join_by(x1km_square)`


Convert the data to long format for plotting.

blackberries_long <- blackberries |>
  select(
    x1km_square,
    mean_insect_mass,
    detected,
    dominant_family
  ) |>
  mutate(detected_char = as.character(detected)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(
      detected_char,
      dominant_family
    ),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  )

Plot box plots for each explanatory variable.

ggplot(
  blackberries_long,
  aes(x = value, y = mean_insect_mass, fill = value)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_x") +
  theme_bw()








Perform a two-way ANOVA.

lm_blackberries <- lm(mean_insect_mass ~ detected * dominant_family, data = blackberries)
blackberry_anova <- anova(lm_blackberries)
print(blackberry_anova)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: mean_insect_mass
                         Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
detected                  1  668.5  668.46 10.7853  0.001609 ** 
dominant_family           3 2800.3  933.44 15.0606 1.222e-07 ***
detected:dominant_family  2  304.6  152.32  2.4577  0.093099 .  
Residuals                69 4276.5   61.98                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


There is evidence that mean insect mass differs according to the presence or absence of R. fruticosus (\(F\)(1, 69) = 10.79, \(p\) = 0.0016) and according to dominant insect family (\(F\)(3, 69) = 15.06, \(p\) = 0.00000012). There is no evidence of an interaction between R. fruticosus presence and dominant insect family (\(F\)(2, 69) = 2.46, \(p\) = 0.0931). Therefore, there is no evidence that the relationship between dominant insect family and mean insect mass differs depending on whether R. fruticosus is present.





Members of the plant order Rosales are popular with hoverflies (members of the family Syrphidae). Test the hypothesis that having Rosales as the dominant flower order (you will need to create a new column based on the column dominant_flower_order) is associated with having members of the hoverfly family (Syrphidae) as the dominant insect family as opposed to members of the bee family Apidae (column dominant_family, you will need to filter to include only these families).







AnswerAnswer






Add a column showing the presence or absence of Rosales as the dominant flower order to the site metadata data frame and filter to include only Apidae and Syrphidae.

rosales <- site_metadata |>
  mutate(rosales_dom = dominant_flower_order == "Rosales") |>
  filter(dominant_family %in% c("Apidae", "Syrphidae"))

Count the groups for the plot.

rosales_counts <- rosales |>
  count(rosales_dom, dominant_family)

Plot a bar chart of the data.

ggplot(rosales_counts, aes(x = rosales_dom, y = n, fill = dominant_family)) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_bw()








Make a contingency table.

cont_table <- xtabs(
  ~ rosales_dom + dominant_family,
  data = rosales
)
print(cont_table)

           dominant_family
rosales_dom Apidae Syrphidae
      FALSE     25        26
      TRUE       9         7


Perform a chi-squared test.

cs <- chisq.test(cont_table)
print(cs)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  cont_table
X-squared = 0.047585, df = 1, p-value = 0.8273


There is no evidence of an association between dominant insect family (Apidae vs Syrphidae) and having Rosales as the dominant flower order (\(\chi^2\)(1) = 0.05, \(p\) = 0.8273)





Different habitat types may favour smaller or larger insects. Test the hypothesis that mean insect mass (mean_insect_mass) differs among habitat types (broad_habitat).







AnswerAnswer






Plot mean insect mass for each habitat type.

ggplot(
  site_metadata,
  aes(x = broad_habitat, y = mean_insect_mass, fill = broad_habitat)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw()








Perform a one-way ANOVA.

lm_hab <- lm(mean_insect_mass ~ broad_habitat, data = site_metadata)
hab_anova <- anova(lm_hab)
print(hab_anova)

Now we can fit the linear model.
ht_lm <- lm(
  min_temp_coldest_month ~ detected,
  data = ht_df,
)
The R function predict() can be used to predict the mean value of the response variable under a fitted linear model given a specific value of the explanatory variable.
Let’s predict minimum temperature for sites where H. tumulorum is present.
new_expl <- tibble(detected = TRUE)

pred <- predict(
  ht_lm,
  newdata = new_expl,
  interval = "confidence"
)

print(pred)

       fit      lwr    upr
1 1.374796 1.068391 1.6812
The values in the fit column are the predicted minimum temperature with H. tumulorum present, and lwr (lower) and upr (upper) are the lower and upper confidence interval of the prediction.
We can extract the standard deviation from the model (using the function sigma()) and plot the predicted distribution. This linear model assumes that observations are normally distributed around the expected value, with a common residual standard deviation
pred_ht <- rnorm(1000, pred[1, "fit"], sigma(ht_lm))

df_ht <- tibble(data = pred_ht)

ggplot(
  df_ht,
  aes(x = data)
) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  theme_bw()
The model therefore gives us more than a single predicted value. For each value of the explanatory variable, it estimates the mean of a probability distribution for the response variable. For a linear model, observations are assumed to be normally distributed around this mean, with the residual standard deviation estimated by sigma().
You can make predictions using a linear model with a continuous explanatory variable by using predict() in exactly the same way. If there are multiple explanatory variables, the value of each variable needs to be passed to the model, the process is otherwise identical.

title: Part 1: Introduction to Bioconductor and Sequence Analysis in R
text:
Endogenous retroviruses
↑ top
Retroviruses are RNA viruses that replicate by converting their RNA genome into DNA. As part of their life cycle, retroviruses integrate this DNA into the genome of their vertebrate host, inserting a copy of their retroviral genome into the host genome.






Figure 29.1: Retrovirus integration



Usually, this happens in a somatic cell, and the virus dies with the host. However, occasionally by chance it will happen in a germline cell, in which case the retrovirus can be inherited as part of the host genome. These inherited retroviruses are known as endogenous retroviruses (ERVs).
Although integration into a germline cell is rare for any individual virus infection, over millions of years of evolution these events accumulate and become relatively common, for example, 5% of the human genome is derived from ERVs.
Endogenous retroviruses are interesting partly because, after integration, they evolve at the slow evolutionary rate of the host instead of the very fast rate we see for viruses. This means that integrated historic viruses can still resemble the original circulating virus for millions, or even hundreds of millions of years. Endogenous retroviruses are one of our best sources of information about the evolutionary history of retroviruses and are sometimes referred to as “molecular fossils” of historical viruses.
Endogenous retroviruses in humans are fairly well known, but we know almost nothing about the retroviruses in the genomes of other species. For example, our recent analyses have revealed that the genome of the North American beaver, Castor canadensis, contains a very large number of endogenous retroviruses, but nobody has looked at these in detail.






Figure 29.2: Castor canadensis

title: Part 1: Introduction to Bioconductor and Sequence Analysis in R
text:
The Practical
↑ top
The aim of this practical is to generate new biological knowledge by analysing endogenous retrovirus sequences from the North American beaver, using bioinformatics techniques. We will upload the annotations generated during this practical to a new publicly available database of mammalian endogenous retroviruses, for the research community to use in the future.

Input
Our start point will be regions of the beaver genome which have previously been identified as likely containing ERVs. Each student will characterise one ERV region, and together the class will build a larger collection of well-characterised ERVs.


Steps
In order to characterise the ERVs we will:

Isolate the sequences from the ERV-like regions
Identify open reading frames (ORFs) in the sequences.
Find out if these ORFs resemble retroviral genes, and if so, which genes.
Find the closest related retroviruses using BLAST and build a multiple sequence alignment and phylogenetic tree
Estimate the age of the ERV using a pairwise sequence alignment.



Output
At the end of the practical you can upload your results to a public database to be used by the research community.

Bioconductor
↑ top
Bioconductor is a repository for R packages, datasets and workflows which are specific for analysing biological data.






Figure 29.3: Bioconductor logo



We are going to use several Bioconductor packages for biological sequence analysis, Biostrings, ORFik, msa, ggtree.
Import these libraries into your Quarto document. We will also need the gt and tidyverse libraries.

library(Biostrings)
library(ORFik)
library(msa)
library(ggtree)
library(gt)
library(tidyverse)

section: Isolate sequences from the ERV-like regions
text:
Isolate sequences from the ERV-like regions
↑ top
You have been provided with sequence data from the beaver genome in FASTA format as data/C_canadensis_erv_regions.fasta. This file contains the DNA sequence of 365 regions of the beaver genome which have previously been identified as potentially containing ERVs.
FASTA is a simple text-based format commonly used for storing biological sequences, such as DNA, RNA or protein sequences.
Each sequence in a FASTA file consists of two parts:

A sequence identifier (or name), which begins with a > symbol.
On the following line or lines, the biological sequence itself.

A FASTA file can one or many contain many sequences. Each sequence starts with a new identifier line followed by a line break, then its sequence, then another line break.
e.g. 
>Sequence1
AGCTATGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTA
>Sequence2
TTCAGCTGATTCTGATCTACTA
Open the FASTA file provided in the data directory as data/C_canadensis_erv_regions.fasta in a text editor on your computer.

title: Part 2: Finding Open Reading Frames
text:
Retrovirus genes
↑ top
Now we have our sequence, we want to check if it really does contain an ERV.
All retroviruses have three genes in common (some also have additional genes):
When the retrovirus first enters the host genome, it will be identical to the viral genome. However, over time, the retrovirus will pick up mutations and become less and less recognisable.
crumbs: 30  Part 2: Finding Open Reading Frames

title: Part 2: Finding Open Reading Frames
text:
gag - group-specific antigen - encodes structural proteins (1500-1800 nt).
pol - polymerase - encodes enzymes required for viral replication (2500-3500 nt).
env - envelope - encodes surface proteins which allow the virus to attach to host cells (2500-3000 nt).
crumbs: 30  Part 2: Finding Open Reading Frames

title: Part 2: Finding Open Reading Frames
text:
Open Reading Frames
↑ top
When a retrovirus first integrates into the host genome, its copy in the host genome will contain intact, full length open reading frames (ORFs) for at least gag, pol and env.
An ORF is a stretch of DNA that could potentially encode a protein. It typically begins with a start codon and continues until the next stop codon.
When we translate a sequence, it can be translated in 3 reading frames on each strand.
For example, lets say we have the sequence below:

my_seq <- DNAStringSet("ATATGAAACCCGGGTTTTAAGC")







Note



In reality, DNA is transcribed into RNA before being translated, however for convenience in R we can directly translate DNA sequences.


Our sequence can be divided into codons as follows:
frame 1:
ATA TGA AAC CCG GGT TTT AAG C
 I   *   N   P   G   F   K

frame 2:
AT ATG AAA CCC GGG TTT TAA GC
    M   K   P   G   F   *
frame 3:
A TAT GAA ACC CGG GTT TTA AGC
   Y   E   T   R   V   L   S
Here, the only open reading frame is in frame 2, where there is a start codon, ATG, encoding methionine (M), followed by four more amino acids, then a stop codon (*), TAA.
We can detect ORFs in R using the findORFs() function from the package ORFik.

# the [[1]] here is because this function can work on multiple
# sequences at once - we only have one sequence so we only want
# the first result.
my_orfs <- findORFs(my_seq)[[1]]

print(my_orfs)

IRanges object with 1 range and 0 metadata columns:
          start       end     width
      <integer> <integer> <integer>
  [1]         3        20        18


The result is an IRanges object which shows us there is an ORF running from the start codon at position 3 to the stop codon at position 20, with a width of 18 nucleotides.

ORFs in the ERV sequence






ExerciseExercise 1







Find ORFs in your ERV sequence (stored in the variable current_erv) using the findORFs function. As in the example, you will need to add [[1]] at the end, as you only have a single sequence.
The longest ORFs in the sequence are likely to represent the retroviral genes, so we can add the argument minimumLength = 200 to filter out ORFs less than 200 amino acids in length.
Store the result in a variable named orfs.






AnswerAnswer







orfs <- findORFs(current_erv, minimumLength = 200)[[1]]









Have a look at your orfs variable, it is an IRanges object showing the start and end positions of the ORFs within the longer sequence, along with their width (the length of the ORF in nucleotides).

print(orfs)

IRanges object with 5 ranges and 0 metadata columns:
          start       end     width
      <integer> <integer> <integer>
  [1]      2287      2964       678
  [2]      3638      4327       690
  [3]      7688      8410       723
  [4]      1401      2321       921
  [5]      5307      6008       702




Adding sequence names
Currently, our ORFs don’t have names, so it may be hard to identify which is which later.
The paste0 function in R concatenates two or more arguments into a single character variable.
e.g.

print(paste0("abc", 1))

[1] "abc1"


If one of the arguments to paste0 is a vector, R will combine each element of the vector with the other arguments.






Note



Remember that the function seq(start, end, increment) generates a vector of numbers from start to end with a step size of increment, e.g. seq(1, 10, 2) = 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.


e.g. 

print(paste0("abc", seq(1, 10)))

 [1] "abc1"  "abc2"  "abc3"  "abc4"  "abc5"  "abc6"  "abc7"  "abc8"  "abc9" 
[10] "abc10"








ExerciseExercise 2







Generate a vector to use as unique names for your ORFs using the paste0 function. They should be named ‘Ccan_ERV_j_ORF_i’ where j is the ID of your specific ERV region and i is a unique number for each ORF. You can find out how many ORFs you have using the function length(orfs) and generate the sequence of numbers using seq(). Store the names as a variable orf_names.






AnswerAnswer







# Replace ERV_1 with the ID of your specific ERV region
orf_names <- paste0("Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_", seq(1, length(orfs)))









You can assign these names to the ORFs in your IRanges variable as follows:

names(orfs) <- orf_names

Have another look at the resulting variable - the ORFs should now have unique names.

print(orfs)

To do so, we can use the function extractAt().

# Again this function can work on multiple sequences at once
# We only have one sequence so we only want the first result, hence the [[1]].
orf_seqs <- extractAt(current_erv, orfs)[[1]]

print(orf_seqs)

title: Part 3: Identifying Sequences with BLAST
text:
Finding related sequences using BLAST
↑ top
Now we have our amino acid sequences, we want to check if they are derived from retroviruses. We can do this using the online BLAST server, with the BLASTp algorithm, which compares protein sequences with protein sequences.
We will compare our ORF sequences with a database of known retrovirus proteins to find out:
A FASTA file of the amino acid sequences of known retroviral genes has been provided for you in data/known_ERV_proteins.fasta.
On the BLASTp homepage, first select the checkbox “Align 2 or more sequences”. This is because both our query sequences and our database sequences are stored in local FASTA files. The alternative is to search against one of the large online databases provided by NCBI.
Your query sequences are the sequences you want to identify - your putative ERV ORFs. Click the “Browse…” button in the query sequence section and choose the FASTA file you just created - output/orf_aa_seqs.fasta.
The subject sequences are the database you would like to compare to - the known retrovirus gene sequences. Click the “Browse…” button in the subject sequence section and choose the FASTA file of known retrovirus sequences - data/known_ERV_proteins.fasta.
Otherwise, the default options are OK. Click the “BLAST” button.

title: Part 3: Identifying Sequences with BLAST
text:
Which retroviral genes we can identify.
What type of retrovirus they are derived from.
What are the most closely related known retroviruses?









Figure 31.1: The BLASTp homepage











Figure 31.2: BLASTp setup
crumbs: 31  Part 3: Identifying Sequences with BLAST

title: Part 3: Identifying Sequences with BLAST
text:
BLAST Results
↑ top
Once BLAST has finished running, you should see something like this:






Figure 31.3: BLASTp results



The dropdown box next to “Results for” allows you to choose which of your ORFs you would like to see the results for.






Note



It’s possible that some of your ORFs will have no results, if so that’s fine - that just means that specific ORF is unlikely to be derived from a retrovirus.


Further down on the page, you should see a table showing all of the database sequences (or the top 100, if there are more than 100) which were significantly more similar to your query sequence than would be expected by chance.






Figure 31.4: BLASTp table



The columns in this table are as follows:







Column
Meaning




Cluster Representative Sequence
The ID and name of this subject sequence.


Max Score
The highest local alignment score for a single high-scoring segment between your query and this subject sequence. Higher is better.


Total Score
The combined score of all aligned segments between your query and this subject sequence. Higher is generally better.


Query Cover
The percentage of your query sequence that is included in the alignment. Higher is better.


E value
The expected number of matches of this quality that could occur by chance in a database of this size. Lower is better; values close to zero indicate more significant matches.


Per. Ident
The percentage of aligned positions that are identical between your query and the matching sequence. Higher is better.


Acc. Len
The total length of this subject sequence in the database.


Accession
The unique identifier for this subject sequence in the database, which can be used to retrieve more information about it.



When evaluating BLAST results, you should consider several columns together. In general, a good match will have a high query cover, high percentage identity, and a low E value.
The subject retrovirus sequence names also provide some information. They are formatted as identifier|name|genus|gene, where:

identifier is a unique identifer for the sequence
name is the name of the retrovirus
genus is gamma, beta, alpha, epsilon, delta, lenti or spuma - these are the different genera of retroviruses - the taxonomic groups to which they belong.
gene is gag, pol or env - the retroviral gene which matches this ORF

For example, if I had the results below:






Figure 31.5: BLASTp table



Then my results for this ORF are:

Most similar sequence name: Bat endogenous retrovirus
Most similar sequence accesion: JQ303225
Most similar retroviral genus: gamma
Most similar retroviral gene: pol







ExerciseExercise 1







Record the most similar sequence name for each ORF in an R data frame with two columns - name and most_similar_sequence_id (as we did in Data Frames). Name the data frame variable blast_res.






AnswerAnswer







blast_res <- tibble(
  name = names(orfs),
  most_similar_sequence_id = c(
    "JQ303225|Bat_Endogenous_Retrovirus|gamma|gag",
    "JQ303225|Bat_Endogenous_Retrovirus|gamma|pol",
    "AY099324|Porcine_ERV_B|gamma|env",
    "JQ303225|Bat_Endogenous_Retrovirus|gamma|gag",
    "JQ303225|Bat_Endogenous_Retrovirus|gamma|gag"
  )
)















Important



At this point, please save the BLAST results from the web server onto your computer in FASTA format.
To do this, for each of your query sequences, select Download at the top of the hit table, then select FASTA (aligned clusters).
 This will save a file on your computer named seqdump.txt Move this file to your output folder for this practical and rename it as Ccan_ERV_j_ORF_i_refs.fasta, replacing j with your ERV ID and i with your ORF ID.
You’ll need to repeat this process for each of your ORFs.

title: Part 3: Identifying Sequences with BLAST
text:
Review
↑ top
At this stage, we know quite a lot about our ERVs:

Which retroviral genes are present.
The location of the longest ORF for each gene within our source sequence.
Which retroviral genus each gene is likely to be derived from.
Which known retrovirus each gene is most similar to.

There are several things here which could mean your results are extra interesting:

Genes from more than one different genus in your identified ERV ORF set - this suggests that the retrovirus could be a recombinant generated by recombination between two different viruses.
Most ERVs in mammals are of the gamma, beta or spuma genus - alpha and epsilon like ERVs are rarer and delta and lenti like ERVs are very rare so any non-gamma/beta ERVs in beavers would be very interesting.

However, even if neither of these are true, you are still most likely the first scientist to find out anything about your specific ERV!
↑ top






NoteSummary




BLAST uses local alignment to identify sequences in a database which are similar to a query.
BLAST results include various important information
Database columns can be split on a delimiter using separate_wider_delim().
slice_max() can be used to select rows from a grouped data frame with the largest value in a specific column.

Build multiple sequence alignments
↑ top
Now, for each retroviral gene, we have identified an ORF, its location and sequence, and have used BLASTp to identify its most similar known retroviral proteins and likely genus.

We can now align each gene sequence with the protein sequences of the same gene from other retroviruses in a multiple sequence alignment and then build a phylogeny to see the evolutionary relationships between our sequences and their relatives.
To build these multiple sequence alignments, we first need to build AAStringSet objects for each gene, containing the ORF we identified for that gene along with the sequences of known retrovirus proteins from the same gene and genus, which we identified earlier using BLASTp.
I will take you through this process with one of my ORFs, Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4, which is a gag gene from the gamma genus.
First, I will create an AAStringSet with just this one sequence.
identified_current <- identified_orf_seqs["Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4"]

print(identified_current)

AAStringSet object of length 1:
    width seq                                               names               
[1]   307 MRVRVGARPWLASLINSALLIAF...ARNHPSLVNSFSDSPLQFGSRG* Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4
Then, I will read file output/Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4.fasta, generated earlier when I saved my BLAST output as a FASTA file, into a second AAStringSet with the readAAStringSet() function.
refs_current <- readAAStringSet("output/Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4_refs.fasta")
I can combine these two AAStringSets using the c (concatenate) function.
combined_current <- c(identified_current, refs_current)

print(combined_current)

Now I can generate a multiple sequence alignment for these sequences directly in R, using the msa() function. We will use the MSA tool Muscle.
msa() outputs a different type of variable (called a MsaAAMultipleAlignment), but we can convert it back to an AAStringSet with the as() function.
combined_current_aligned <- msa(combined_current, method = "Muscle")
combined_current_aligned_ss <- as(combined_current_aligned, "AAStringSet")
I will save the aligned sequences into a new FASTA file, in my output directory, named as gene_Ccan_ERV_j_ORF_i.fasta, replacing gene with the gene I am currently analysing (gag, pol or env), j with my ERV ID and i with my ORF ID.
writeXStringSet(combined_current_aligned_ss, "output/gag_Ccan_ERV_1_ORF_4.fasta")
You can look at this file directly in a text editor, however it’s quite difficult to see details of the alignment in this format. Alternatively, you can upload the sequence to an online alignment viewer, such as Alignment Viewer.

title: Part 4: Multiple Sequence Alignment and Phylogeny
text:
Build phylogenies
↑ top
There are various ways we can create phylogenies from our sequences, including directly inside R. However, in R the options for tree-building algorithms are quite limited.
Instead, we can take our aligned sequences to an external web server to generate a phylogeny. Today we’ll use the IQTREE web server.
IQTREE is a maximum likelihood approach to tree building which allows a specific amino acid substitution model to be specified.
Upload one of your multiple sequence alignments in the Input section.






Figure 32.1: IQTree



In the Options section, choose an amino acid model, RtREV. We would ideally use the find best and apply option to find the best fitting model, however this takes a very long time to run. The RtREV model, based on a retrovirus specific amino acid substitution matrix, is a good compromise in this case.
Please also select Simple midpoint in the “Root tree” section, as we don’t have a specific outgroup sequence in this case.






Figure 32.2: IQTree Options



The default options are OK for our purposes for the other options, so choose Submit.






Note



You may see some warning messages that the sequence names in your phylogeny are not found in the alignment file - this is because IQTree replaces the | symbols in sequence names with _ symbols, and is nothing to worry about.


Once the tree-building algorithm has finished (this might take a couple of minutes), click on Newick in the results section - this will show your tree in Newick format. Paste the text displayed on the next screen into an empty text file and save it in your output directory as gene_Ccan_ERV_j_ORF_i.newick, replacing gene with the gene you are currently analysing (gag, pol or env), j with your ERV ID and i with your ORF ID.






ExerciseExercise 2







Repeat the steps above for each of the ORF sequences in your identified_orf_df data frame, so that you have one Newick file for each gene. Save all of the alignments in NEWICK format with names formatted as above.
